statement: CMS reports 2024 national health spending of 1,634.7 billion dollars on hospitals, 1,109.7 billion on physician and clinical services, 467.0 billion on prescription drugs and 590.5 billion from other third party payers and public health activity.
anchor: Hospital expenditures grew 8.9% to $1,634.7 billion in 2024, slower than the 10.6% growth in 2023.
Physician and clinical services expenditures grew 8.1% to $1,109.7 billion in 2024, faster growth than the 7.4% in 2023.
Prescription drug spending increased 7.9% to $467.0 billion in 2024, slower than the 10.8% growth in 2023.
Other Third Party Payers and Programs and Public Health Activity spending declined 7.0% in 2024 to $590.5 billion, or 11 percent of total NHE.
context: CMS Office of the Actuary, National Health Expenditure Accounts, 2024 data released December 2025; complements EV-CAR-120 and EV-CAR-121, which give the payer lines. The fact sheet text does not give the total on the payer lines, so the model derives the remainder.

statement: CMS projects that over 2025 to 2034 national health spending grows 5.4 percent a year on average, Medicare 7.7 percent a year and both Medicaid and private health insurance 5.0 percent a year, that the insured share of the population is 90.5 percent in 2034, and that the federal share of spending rises from 31 percent to 33 percent.
anchor: Over 2025-34 average NHE growth (5.4 percent) is projected to outpace that of average Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth (4.1 percent), resulting in an increase in the health spending share of GDP from 18.0 percent in 2024 to 20.6 percent in 2034.

Medicare spending is expected to grow the fastest among major sources of funding over 2025-34, at 7.7 percent per year on average. (In contrast, both Medicaid spending and private health insurance (PHI) spending are expected to grow 5.0 percent per year on average over 2025-34.)
The insured share of the population is expected to be 90.5 percent in 2034, compared to 91.8 percent in 2024.
The federal government-sponsored share of NHE is expected to continue to increase from 31 percent in 2024 to 33 percent in 2034.
context: CMS Office of the Actuary projections of national health expenditures, 2025 to 2034, published before the 2025 reconciliation law could be fully reflected and before the 2026 credit expiry; they will differ from CBO on coverage and Medicaid growth. No second publisher is linked: CBO publishes subsidies, not national spending. Re-check when CMS releases the 2025 data around December 2026.

statement: CMS reports that per person personal health care spending in 2020 was 22,356 dollars for people 65 and older, 4,217 dollars for children and 9,154 dollars for working-age people, against 10,191 dollars nationally.
anchor: Per person personal health care spending for the 65 and older population was $22,356 in 2020, over 5 times higher than spending per child ($4,217) and almost 2.5 times the spending per working-age person ($9,154).
Medicaid expenditures per enrollee were highest in North Dakota ($12,314) and lowest in Georgia ($4,754) in 2020.

In 2020, per capita personal health care spending ranged from $7,522 in Utah to $14,007 in New York. Per capita spending in New York state was 37 percent higher than the national average ($10,191) while spending in Utah was about 26 percent lower.
context: CMS Office of the Actuary, NHE by age and sex, 2020. The national average of 10,191 dollars is quoted in the state-of-residence summary. The model uses the age gradient only to scale the cost of covering people aged 50 to 64 and children; a current-year age table would replace it.

CBO restating the HHS guideline; the model uses it to turn income bands into dollars for the premium tax credit schedule.

anchor: The federal government provides about two-thirds of all funding, and states finance the remainder.
context: Congressional Budget Office with the Joint Committee on Taxation staff, report published July 2026 on the February 2026 baseline; nonpartisan; projections assume current law and are uncertain, as the report itself says. Added for the health coverage model (models/tools/health-coverage), which uses the 2032 column. A general description of the matching rules; the share is higher for adults made eligible by the ACA and lower for some other groups.

statement: CBO projects that annual spending per Medicare Advantage enrollee will be 7 percent higher, on average, than spending per fee-for-service enrollee with Parts A and B, that Medicare Advantage will account for 54 percent of Part A and B spending in 2026 and 61 percent in 2036, and that in 2032 spending is 20900 dollars per Medicare Advantage enrollee and 19500 dollars per fee-for-service enrollee.
anchor: 54 percent in 2026 to 61 percent in 2036. Over that period, annual spending per MA enrollee is projected
to be 7 percent higher, on average, than spending per FFS enrollee with both Part A and Part B coverage.
context: Congressional Budget Office with the Joint Committee on Taxation staff, report published July 2026 on the February 2026 baseline; nonpartisan; projections assume current law and are uncertain, as the report itself says. Added for the health coverage model (models/tools/health-coverage), which uses the 2032 column. CBO notes that its estimate includes supplemental benefits financed through plan rebates and excludes categories always paid through fee-for-service. MedPAC estimates a larger gap (EV-CAR-135).

11.6% of working-age Americans (those ages 18–64), did not have health insurance in 2025
context: NCHS press release 2026-05-28, second Trump administration (CDC/HHS). NHIS measures coverage at the time of interview, so it runs higher than the Census figure of 7.9 percent; the two measure different things.

statement: In 2025 more than 1 in 5 Hispanic adults ages 18-64 (21.9%) lacked health insurance, against 11.3% of Black, 8.5% of White and 4.9% of Asian non-Hispanic adults.
anchor: more than 1 in 5 Hispanic adults ages 18–64 (21.9%) lacked health insurance, a greater percentage than Black, non-Hispanic adults (11.3%); White, non-Hispanic adults (8.5%) and Asian, non-Hispanic adults (4.9%)
context: NCHS press release 2026-05-28, second Trump administration (CDC/HHS); NHIS.

statement: Adults ages 18-64 in states that had not expanded Medicaid were almost twice as likely to be uninsured (18.1%) in 2025 as those in expansion states (9.0%).
anchor: Adults ages 18–64 who live in states that had not expanded Medicaid were almost twice as likely to be uninsured (18.1%) in 2025 compared to those living in states that had expanded Medicaid (9.0%)
context: NCHS press release 2026-05-28, second Trump administration (CDC/HHS); NHIS. A difference between groups of states, not a causal estimate of expansion.

statement: In 2026, 46 percent of working-age adults were inadequately insured: 11 percent were uninsured, 12 percent had a coverage gap during the year, and 23 percent were underinsured.
anchor: Nearly half of working-age adults, 46 percent, were inadequately insured in 2026: 11 percent were uninsured, 12 percent had a coverage gap during the year, and 23 percent were underinsured, meaning they had coverage but their plan didn’t provide affordable access to care.
context: Commonwealth Fund (private foundation), published 2026-10-22; SSRS telephone and online survey of 9,360 adults, May-July 2026. The Fund favors coverage expansion; the underinsurance threshold (out-of-pocket costs or deductible at 5 to 10 percent of income) is the Fund's own definition. Survey fielded after the end of the enhanced marketplace subsidies and before the H.R. 1 Medicaid changes.

statement: The Commonwealth Fund survey found the uninsured rate for working-age adults rose from 8.9 percent in 2024 to 11.2 percent in 2026, with marketplace and individual coverage falling from 8.5 percent to 6.4 percent.
anchor: The uninsured rate for working-age adults increased from 8.9 percent in 2024 to 11.2 percent in 2026.
from 8.5 percent in 2024 to 6.4 percent in 2026
context: Commonwealth Fund survey, 2026-10-22. The Fund notes its estimate runs above federal surveys; it is the only source in this batch that already reflects the 2026 loss of enhanced marketplace subsidies, and it contrasts with the flat federal 2025 figures (EV-CAR-100, EV-CAR-104), which cover an earlier year.

statement: In 2026, 30 percent of working-age adults insured all year were underinsured, including 29 percent of people with employer-sponsored insurance and half of people in marketplace plans.
anchor: In 2026, 30 percent of working-age adults who were insured all year were underinsured by this definition. This includes 29 percent of people with employer-sponsored insurance and half of people in marketplace plans.
context: Commonwealth Fund, 2026-10-22; Fund-defined measure of underinsurance.

statement: The share of working-age adults who delayed or avoided health care because of cost rose from 46 percent in 2022 to 50 percent in 2026.
anchor: More people delayed or avoided getting health care because of the cost, with the rate climbing from 46 percent in 2022 to 50 percent in 2026.
context: Commonwealth Fund survey, 2026-10-22.

statement: Annual premiums for employer-sponsored family health coverage reached $28,303 in 2026, 5% higher than in 2025.
anchor: Annual premiums for employer-sponsored family health coverage reached $28,303 this year, 5% higher than in 2025.
context: KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey, published 2026-10-22, 1,937 firms; nonpartisan. Survey estimate, not administrative data.

statement: On average, covered workers contributed $7,471 toward the cost of family coverage in 2026.
anchor: On average, covered workers contributed $7,471 toward the cost of family coverage.
context: KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey, 2026-10-22.

statement: The average deductible among covered workers in a plan with a general annual deductible was $1,955 for single coverage in 2026.
anchor: The average deductible among covered workers in a plan with a general annual deductible was $1,955 for single coverage.
context: KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey, 2026-10-22.

statement: KFF reports that, heading into 2027, forecasts again project employer premium increases approaching double digits.
anchor: Heading into 2027, forecasts are again projecting premium increases approaching double digits.
context: KFF, 2026-10-22, reporting third-party forecasts, not its own projection; no numeric forecast is quoted.

statement: About three in ten adults (28%) skipped or postponed needed health care in the past 12 months because of cost, and roughly six in ten uninsured adults (62%) did so.
anchor: Roughly three in ten adults (28%) say that they have skipped or postponed getting needed health care in the past 12 months because of the cost.
roughly six in ten (62%) uninsured adults say they have skipped or postponed getting the health care they needed due to cost
context: KFF brief updated 2026-10-23 from the KFF Survey of Health Access and Caregiving; nonpartisan. The NHIS-based figure for 2024 is lower (17 percent, KFF analysis) because it measures delay or non-receipt more narrowly.

statement: CFPB research shows $88 billion in medical debt on consumer credit records as of June 2021.
anchor:
CFPB research shows $88 billion in medical debt on consumer credit records as of June
2021.
context: CFPB, March 2022, Biden administration; analysis of the CFPB Consumer Credit Panel. The report says the true total is likely higher because not all medical debt in collections reaches the credit bureaus.

statement: As of 2021, 58 percent of all third-party debt collection tradelines on credit records were for medical debt, the most common collection type.
anchor:
As of 2021, 58 percent of all third-party debt collection tradelines were for medical debt,
making medical debt the most common debt collection tradeline on credit records.
context: CFPB, March 2022, Biden administration; Consumer Credit Panel.

statement: A KFF poll found about 41% of adults have health care debt, which KFF Health News and NPR reported as more than 100 million people in America.
anchor: more than 100 million people in America ― including 41% of adults ― beset by a health care system that is systematically pushing patients into debt on a mass scale
context: KFF Health News and NPR, 2022-06-16, journalism built on a KFF survey of 2,375 adults. The 100 million is a journalistic extrapolation from the 41% share; the survey counts any money owed for medical or dental bills, including credit-card and family loans, a much broader measure than the CFPB credit-report figure. Data are from early 2022.

statement: A Census Bureau analysis of the 2020 Survey of Income and Program Participation found that 17% of households owed medical debt in 2019.
anchor: A recent Census Bureau analysis of data from the 2020 Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) on medical debt at the household level found 17% of households owed medical debt in 2019.
locator: Section on measuring health care debt
context: Reported by KFF (2022-06-16); the Census analysis itself was not retrieved, so this is a secondhand citation of official data.

statement: NHE grew 7.2% to $5.3 trillion in 2024, or $15,474 per person, and accounted for 18.0% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
anchor: NHE grew 7.2% to $5.3 trillion in 2024, or $15,474 per person, and accounted for 18.0% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
context: CMS Office of the Actuary, National Health Expenditure Accounts, 2024 data released December 2025, second Trump administration. The 2025 NHE is due around December 2026 and was not available.

statement: Private health insurance spending reached $1,644.6 billion in 2024 (31 percent of NHE), Medicare $1,118.0 billion (21 percent), Medicaid $931.7 billion (18 percent), and out-of-pocket spending $556.6 billion (11 percent).
anchor: Medicare spending grew 7.8% to $1,118.0 billion in 2024, or 21 percent of total NHE.
Medicaid spending grew 6.6% to $931.7 billion in 2024, or 18 percent of total NHE.
Private health insurance spending grew 8.8% to $1,644.6 billion in 2024, or 31 percent of total NHE.
Out of pocket spending grew 5.9% to $556.6 billion in 2024, or 11 percent of total NHE.
context: CMS Office of the Actuary, second Trump administration.

statement: CMS projects NHE growth to average 5.4 percent a year over 2025-34 against 4.1 percent for GDP, raising health spending from 18.0 percent of GDP in 2024 to 20.6 percent in 2034.
anchor: Over 2025-34 average NHE growth (5.4 percent) is projected to outpace that of average Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth (4.1 percent), resulting in an increase in the health spending share of GDP from 18.0 percent in 2024 to 20.6 percent in 2034.
context: CMS Office of the Actuary projection (published June 2026, second Trump administration), a current-law baseline that includes H.R. 1; an agency projection, not data. No independent projection from another publisher was read for this batch.

statement: CMS projects the insured share of the population at 90.5 percent in 2034, compared with 91.8 percent in 2024.
anchor: The insured share of the population is expected to be 90.5 percent in 2034, compared to 91.8 percent in 2024.
context: CMS Office of the Actuary projection, second Trump administration, under current law including H.R. 1.

statement: The United States spends $14 885 per capita on health, more than the OECD average of $5 967 (USD PPP).
anchor:
The United States spends $14 885 per capita on health, more than the OECD average of $5 967
(USD PPP).
context: OECD Health at a Glance 2025 country note (November 2025, CC BY 4.0); OECD Health Statistics from national sources. The OECD figure includes capital spending, so it differs from the Peterson-KFF consumption-only figure.

statement: The United States health spending equals 17.2% of GDP, compared with 9.3% on average in the OECD.
anchor: This is equal to 17.2% of GDP, compared to 9.3% on average in the OECD.
context: OECD, November 2025, CC BY 4.0. CMS reports 18.0% of GDP for the same year on its own accounting (EV-CAR-120); the difference is definitional.

statement: Life expectancy in the United States was 78.4 years, 2.7 years below the OECD average.
anchor: In the United States, life expectancy was 78.4 years, 2.7 years below the OECD average.
context: OECD country note, November 2025; refers to 2023 data. CDC final 2024 data show 79.0 years (EV-CAR-139), so the gap is somewhat smaller on newer data.

statement: Preventable mortality was 217 per 100 000 in the United States, above the OECD average of 145, and treatable mortality was 95 per 100 000, above the OECD average of 77.
anchor:
Preventable mortality was 217 per 100 000 in the United States (higher than the OECD average of
145); with treatable mortality at 95 per 100 000 (higher than the OECD average of 77).
context: OECD country note, November 2025. Preventable and treatable mortality are the OECD components of avoidable mortality.

statement: In 2024 the U.S. spent 17.2% of GDP on health, substantially more than peer countries, which average 11.2% of GDP.
anchor: In 2024, the U.S. spent 17.2% of GDP on health – still substantially higher than peer countries, which average 11.2% of GDP.
locator: Health consumption as percent of GDP
context: Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker, published 2026-03-11; KFF analysis of OECD data for 11 comparable countries and CMS data for the U.S. Uses health consumption spending, which excludes investment.

statement: The U.S. spends nearly twice as much on health care per person as peer nations ($13,432 vs. $7,393), while utilization is generally lower, so higher prices rather than higher utilization explain the gap.
anchor: The U.S. spends nearly twice as much on health care per person as peer nations ($13,432 vs. $7,393 per person), meanwhile health care utilization in the U.S. — from doctor visits to surgeries — is generally lower than in other wealthy countries.
higher prices – as opposed to higher utilization – explain the United States’ high health spending relative to other high-income countries
context: KFF/Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker, updated 2025-09-04; KFF analysis of OECD data for 11 peer countries. The price-versus-use attribution is KFF's interpretation.

statement: Commonwealth Fund's Mirror, Mirror 2024 ranks the United States last overall among the countries compared, with Australia, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom the top three.
anchor: The United States ranks last overall (Exhibits 1 and 2). The three top-performing countries in 2024 are Australia, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom.
context: Commonwealth Fund, 2024-09-19. A composite index of 70 measures in five domains with the Fund's own weighting; the Fund favors universal coverage. The same report ranks the U.S. second on care process, so the overall rank hides strengths.

statement: Across all hospital inpatient and outpatient services in 2022, employers and private insurers paid on average 254 percent of what Medicare would have paid for the same services at the same facilities.
anchor: employers and private insurers paid on average 254 percent of what Medicare would have paid for the same services at the same facilities in 2022
context: RAND Corporation, Round 5 report, 2024-05-13; employer-led study, not peer reviewed. It covers about 6 percent of commercial hospital spending, from 12 state all-payer claims databases and self-insured employers, and excludes Maryland. Medicare-based benchmarks are a yardstick, not a measure of cost.

statement: U.S. insurers and providers spent $812 billion on administration in 2017, $2497 per capita or 34.2% of national health expenditures, versus $551 per capita (17.0%) in Canada.
anchor: U.S. insurers and providers spent $812 billion on administration, amounting to $2497 per capita (34.2% of national health expenditures) versus $551 per capita (17.0%) in Canada
context: Annals of Internal Medicine, 2020-01-07, peer reviewed (Himmelstein, Campbell, Woolhandler). Data are from 2017. The authors are single-payer advocates; the estimate counts a wide set of administrative functions. Other estimates (McKinsey, CBO) were not read for this batch. The abstract notes accounting categories differ somewhat between the two countries.

statement: In 2025, 55 percent of eligible Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage, up from 37 percent in 2018, with about 34.9 million enrollees and an estimated $537 billion in plan payments.
anchor:
In 2025, 55 percent of eligible Medicare
beneficiaries enrolled in MA, up from 54 percent in 2024 and 37 percent
in 2018. In 2025, the MA program included 5,492 plan options offered by
164 organizations, enrolled about 34.9 million beneficiaries, and paid MA
plans an estimated $537 billion
context: MedPAC (nonpartisan congressional advisory commission), March 12 2026; counts based on CMS enrollment files, excluding beneficiaries without both Part A and Part B.

statement: In 2026, 55% of eligible Medicare beneficiaries, 35.2 million out of 64.2 million with both Parts A and B, are enrolled in Medicare Advantage.
anchor: In 2026, more than half (55%) of eligible Medicare beneficiaries – 35.2 million out of 64.2 million Medicare beneficiaries with both Medicare Parts A and B – are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans
context: KFF analysis of CMS enrollment files, published 2026-06-05; nonpartisan. Newer than the MedPAC 2025 count.

statement: MedPAC estimates that in 2026 Medicare will spend 14 percent, a projected $76 billion, more for Medicare Advantage enrollees than it would if they were in fee-for-service Medicare.
anchor:
We estimate that Medicare will spend 14 percent—a projected $76 billion—
more for MA enrollees in 2026 than it would spend if those beneficiaries were
enrolled in FFS Medicare
context: MedPAC, March 12 2026. The Commission says this is not an estimate of plan profit; the extra funds supplemental benefits. The estimate follows from favorable selection and coding intensity and depends on MedPAC's method. It is lower than last year's 20 percent estimate (EV-CAR-136) because the V28 risk model finished phasing in.

statement: MedPAC projected in 2025 that Medicare would spend 20 percent more on Medicare Advantage enrollees than on similar enrollees in fee-for-service Medicare.
anchor:
Last year, we projected that in 2025, Medicare would spend 20 percent more
on MA enrollees than on similar enrollees in FFS Medicare.
context: MedPAC, March 2026 report restating its March 2025 estimate. The method changed in the 2026 report (end-stage renal disease enrollees now included), so the 20 and 14 percent figures are not strictly comparable.

statement: Traditional Medicare has no annual limit on out-of-pocket spending for Part A and Part B services, while Medicare Advantage plans must cap in-network costs at no more than $9,250 in 2026.
anchor: Traditional Medicare does not include an annual limit on how much beneficiaries pay out-of-pocket for Part A and Part B services.
In 2026, this limit may not exceed $9,250 for in-network services
locator: Section: Traditional Medicare has No Out-of-Pocket Limit
context: KFF, 2026-10-09; nonpartisan description of program rules, a secondary source for law. Most traditional Medicare beneficiaries hold Medigap or retiree coverage, which KFF says averaged $2,604 a year in premiums in 2023 (not quoted here).

statement: Medicaid pays for more than two-thirds of long-term care delivered in home- and community-based settings, and in all years since 2016 at least 0.5 million people have been on waiting or interest lists, with almost 650,000 in 2026.
anchor: Medicaid is the primary payer for long-term care (LTC) in the U.S. and pays for more than two-thirds of the LTC delivered in home- and community-based settings.
In all years since 2016, there have been at least 0.5 million people on waiting lists or interest lists, with a total of almost 650,000 in 2026.
context: KFF 24th survey of state Medicaid home care officials (April-August 2026), published 2026-10-05; nonpartisan. Florida and South Carolina did not respond, and prior-year answers were substituted. KFF says waiting lists are an incomplete measure of unmet need and are not comparable across states. The earlier 2025 count was over 600,000.

statement: Life expectancy at birth in the United States was 79.0 years in 2024, an increase of 0.6 year from 78.4 in 2023.
anchor: In 2024, life expectancy at birth was 79.0 years for the total U.S. population—an increase of 0.6 year from 78.4 in 2023
context: NCHS Data Brief 548, January 2026, second Trump administration (CDC/HHS); final death-certificate data. A record high; the 2025 figure was not yet released.

statement: The U.S. maternal mortality rate for 2024 was 17.9 deaths per 100,000 live births (649 deaths), not significantly lower than 18.6 in 2023.
anchor: In 2024, 649 women died of maternal causes in the United States, compared with 669 in 2023
The maternal mortality rate for 2024, 17.9 deaths per 100,000 live births, was not significantly lower than the rate of 18.6 in 2023
context: NCHS Health E-Stat 113, March 2026, second Trump administration (CDC/HHS); vital statistics. Maternal deaths are those within 42 days of the end of pregnancy; counts are small and year-to-year changes are often not significant.

statement: In 2024 the maternal mortality rate for Black non-Hispanic women was 44.8 deaths per 100,000 live births, significantly higher than for White (14.2), Hispanic (12.1) and Asian (18.1) women.
anchor: the maternal mortality rate for Black non-Hispanic (subsequently, Black) women was 44.8 deaths per 100,000 live births, which was significantly higher than the rates for White non-Hispanic (subsequently, White) (14.2), Hispanic (12.1), and Asian non-Hispanic (subsequently, Asian) (18.1) women
context: NCHS Health E-Stat 113, March 2026, second Trump administration (CDC/HHS).

statement: A peer-reviewed study of linked survey and death records found that the ACA Medicaid expansions reduced annual mortality among near-elderly adults by 0.132 percentage points, a 9.4% reduction over the sample mean.
anchor: Individuals in expansion states experienced a 0.132 percentage point decline in annual mortality, a 9.4% reduction over the sample mean, as a result of the Medicaid expansions.
context: Miller, Johnson and Wherry, QJE August 2021; difference-in-differences comparing expansion and non-expansion states, near-elderly low-income adults, effect grows over time. Observational, not randomized; the Oregon lottery found no detectable change in measured physical health in two years (a shorter window and a different population).

statement: In the randomized Oregon lottery, Medicaid coverage produced no statistically significant improvement in measured physical health in the first two years, but lowered the share screening positive for depression by 9.15 percentage points and almost eliminated catastrophic out-of-pocket medical spending.
anchor: Medicaid coverage generated no statistically significant improvements in measured physical health outcomes in the first two years, but did generate increased health care use, higher rates of diabetes detection and management, lower rates of depression, and lower financial strain.
Medicaid coverage decreased the probability of screening positive for depression (-9.15 percentage points; 95% CI: -16.70 to -1.60; P=0.018)
locator: abstract of NEJM 2013 as quoted on NBER publications page
context: Baicker, Finkelstein and colleagues, NEJM 368:1713-1722, May 2013; random assignment by state lottery in 2008, about 12,000 adults surveyed roughly two years later. Critics read the null on blood pressure, cholesterol and glycated hemoglobin as evidence that coverage alone moves physical health slowly; the authors say confidence intervals rule out some effects found in earlier observational studies.

statement: The Oregon experiment found that Medicaid cut the chance of having to borrow money or skip other bills because of medical expenses by 14.2 percentage points from a base of 24.4, and cut catastrophic out-of-pocket spending by 4.5 percentage points from a base of 5.5.
anchor: reducing the chances of having out-of-pocket expenditures that exceeded 30 percent of income by 4.5 percentage points, relative to a base of 5.5)
by 14.2 percentage points, relative to a base of 24.4)
context: Author-written summary of the NEJM 2013 results (Baicker, May 2013); randomized lottery, outcomes about two years after the lottery. Financial-strain results are the strongest and best-replicated Oregon finding.

statement: Urban Institute projected that, without extension of the enhanced premium tax credits, 4.8 million more people would be uninsured in 2026, after Marketplace plan selections reached a record of over 24 million for 2025.
anchor: Marketplace enrollment steadily increased, reaching a new high of over 24 million plan selections for 2025.
Without enhanced PTCs, we project that 4.8 million more people will be uninsured in 2026 relative to a policy that extends enhanced PTCs, an increase in the uninsured population of 21 percent.
context: Urban Institute microsimulation, September 17, 2025, made while Congress debated an extension. Projection, not observed data; compare CBO's lower figure and KFF's 2026 sign-up counts.

statement: CRS reported that CBO projects the uninsured population would increase by 2.2 million in 2026 without an extension of the enhanced premium tax credits, and that subsidized exchange enrollment rose 137% between 2020 and 2025.
anchor: CBO projects that the uninsured population would increase by 2.2 million in 2026 without an extension for that year.
Overall, subsidized exchange enrollment more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, increasing by 137% during this time period.
context: Congressional Research Service FAQ updated December 10, 2025; nonpartisan summary of CBO and JCT estimates. CBO's single-year 2026 figure (2.2 million) is smaller than its multi-year average (3.8 million) and than Urban's 4.8 million.

statement: KFF reported that 2026 Open Enrollment plan sign-ups fell by over a million to 23.1 million, the sharpest single-year drop since the Marketplaces launched, and that effectuated enrollment could fall to about 17.5 million in 2026 from 22.3 million in 2025.
anchor: Plan sign-ups fell by over a million to 23.1 million people during the 2026 Open Enrollment Period, the sharpest single-year drop since the ACA Marketplaces launched.
average monthly effectuated ACA Marketplace enrollment could fall to about 17.5 million people in 2026 and could be as low as 16.5 million people, down from 22.3 million people in 2025.
context: KFF analysis of reported sign-ups and payments, May 19, 2026, the first observed response to expiry of the enhanced credits. The 17.5 million figure is a KFF projection from partial data; KFF says it closely matches CBO's roughly 25% contraction.

statement: Shepard and Wagner found that removing auto-enrollment in the Massachusetts Commonwealth Care exchange, which added one extra step, reduced enrollment by 33 percent and differentially excluded young, healthy and economically disadvantaged people.
anchor: This minor ordeal has a major impact, reducing enrollment by 33 percent and differentially excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
context: American Economic Review, March 2025; natural experiment in 2010 affecting part of the Massachusetts pre-ACA exchange population, which was low-income and eligible for fully subsidized plans. May not transfer to groups who must pay premiums.

statement: CBO projected that if Medicare eligibility were lowered to 60 without automatic enrollment, 53 percent of newly eligible people would enroll in Parts A and B, versus about 82 percent of people ages 65 to 69 in 2019.
anchor: CBO and JCT analyzed a policy that would lower the age of Medicare eligibility from 65 to 60.
53 percent of people newly eligible for Medicare would enroll in Parts A and B, 34 percent would enroll in Part A only, and 13 percent would not enroll in any Medicare coverage.
in 2019, about 82 percent of people ages 65 to 69 enrolled in Parts A and B
context: CBO with JCT staff, May 2022 (nonpartisan). The gap is explained in the text by two things: workers aged 60 to 64 often have employer coverage, and people under 62 would not be automatically enrolled or have premiums withheld. Excerpt only; the cost estimate itself was not read.

statement: CBO projected that 70 percent of the 1.3 million uninsured people newly eligible at age 60 would take up Medicare Parts A and B in 2031, and roughly 80 percent of those taking up coverage would otherwise have no Medicaid or subsidized nongroup option.
anchor: CBO and JCT analyzed a policy that would lower the age of Medicare eligibility from 65 to 60.
70 percent of the 1.3 million people who are uninsured under current law and would be newly eligible for Medicare would take up Medicare Parts A and B in 2031.
Roughly 80 percent of those that would take up coverage under the policy are not eligible for Medicaid or a subsidized nongroup plan under current law
context: CBO and JCT, May 2022. Shows a staged lower-age path reaches a small uninsured group (1.3 million) and mostly displaces employer or nongroup coverage, not uninsurance.

statement: Urban Institute estimated that of 12.0 million people ages 60 to 64 with employer coverage, 9.2 million (77 percent) would keep it with Medicare Part A added, and 2.8 million (23 percent) would drop it, mostly for comprehensive Medicare.
anchor: We estimate that of the 12.0 million people ages 60 to 64 enrolled in employer-sponsored insurance in the baseline for 2023—which assumes the Marketplace subsidies available under the American Rescue Plan Act have been extended and made permanent—9.2 million, or 77 percent, would keep their current coverage with the added benefit of Medicare Part A
The remaining 2.8 million, or 23 percent, would drop their employer-sponsored coverage, with most switching to comprehensive Medicare.
context: Urban Institute, June 2022 (nonpartisan). Baseline assumes ARPA subsidies are permanent, which is not current law in 2029; results should be re-run on the 2029 baseline.

statement: KFF counted at least 25,198,000 Medicaid enrollees disenrolled during the unwinding as of September 12, 2024, and found that 69% of those disenrolled lost coverage for paperwork or procedural reasons.
anchor: As of September 12, 2024, at least 25,198,000 Medicaid enrollees had been disenrolled during the unwinding of the continuous enrollment provision.
Among those who were disenrolled, nearly seven in ten (69%) were disenrolled for paperwork or procedural reasons while three in ten (31%) were determined ineligible.
locator: bullets at top of tracker page
context: KFF compilation of state-reported unwinding data (states report to CMS; reporting differs by state). Procedural share depends on the denominator: KFF notes the rate falls to about one-fifth if all initiated renewals are used (its Sept 2023 explainer gave 73% vs 20%). KFF says many procedurally disenrolled people may still be eligible, but that is not measured here.

statement: At the end of the unwinding, KFF found over 56 million people had coverage renewed, over 25 million were disenrolled (a 31% disenrollment rate), and 61% of renewals were completed through automated ex parte processes.
anchor: over 56 million people had their coverage renewed and over 25 million people have been disenrolled
the overall disenrollment rate during the unwinding was 31%
among those who retained coverage, over six in ten (61%) were renewed through ex parte, or automated, processes.
context: KFF, September 18, 2024; state-reported data, some cases still pending. Evidence that automated renewal protects coverage and that paperwork drives loss when it is missing.

statement: In Arkansas, work requirements were associated with a 13.2 percentage point larger decline in Medicaid or marketplace coverage among adults 30 to 49 than among other age groups, and a 7.1 percentage point rise in the uninsured.
anchor: the percentage of respondents with Medicaid or marketplace coverage declined by 13.2 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], −23.3 to −3.2) more among Arkansans 30 to 49 years of age relative to other age groups in the state
an increase of 7.1 percentage points
context: Sommers et al., NEJM June 2019; telephone survey late 2018 with Kentucky, Louisiana and Texas as comparison states; first 6 months of the policy. Confidence interval is wide (-23.3 to -3.2).

statement: The Arkansas study found no significant change in employment associated with work requirements and that more than 95% of targeted people already met the requirement or should have been exempt.
anchor: We found no significant changes in employment associated with the policy, and more than 95% of persons who were targeted by the policy already met the requirement or should have been exempt.
context: NEJM June 2019. The authors say their confidence intervals are wide enough that policy-relevant employment changes cannot be ruled out; supporters of work requirements argue the longer-run and national effects differ. Study covers the first 6 months only.

statement: KFF reported that in Arkansas about two thirds of enrollees were data matched, about 70% of those who had to report neither obtained an exemption nor reported compliance, and over 18,000 people lost coverage.
anchor: Among those who had to actively report, about 70% did not obtain an exemption or report compliance, ultimately resulting in over 18,000 people losing coverage.
context: KFF, May 20, 2025 (nonpartisan), summarizing state waiver experience while Congress considered a national work requirement. Arkansas state reports are the underlying source.

statement: Georgia's Pathways program, the only Medicaid work requirement applied at application, had 13,369 people enrolled at some point in two years, 8,077 still active two years in, and cost about $110 million through June 2025, with health care benefits about 31% of costs.
anchor: About 13,369 total Georgians had been enrolled in the Pathways to Coverage program at some point during the first two years, which accounts for cumulative enrollment. Only 8,077 of those Georgians were still actively enrolled
Through June 2025 the Pathways to Coverage program cost taxpayers about $110 million
Health care benefits accounted for about 31% of total costs from program approval through the end of year two.
context: Georgia Budget and Policy Institute, October 2025; the institute favors Medicaid expansion (stake). It cites state financial documents; the figures were not checked against those documents here. The state's own reporting and defense of the program were not read.

statement: CBO's report on single-payer design described design choices and trade-offs but did not address every issue in implementing and transitioning to such a system, and did not analyze the budgetary effects of any specific proposal.
anchor: The report does not address all of the issues involved in designing, implementing, and transitioning to a single-payer system, nor does it analyze the budgetary effects of any specific proposal.
context: CBO, May 2019, requested by House Budget Committee Chairman Yarmuth; qualitative. Its numerical work came later (Dec 2020 working paper, 2022 testimony).

statement: CBO staff told the House Budget Committee that the federal cost of administering Medicare was 1.4 percent of Medicare expenditures in 2017, about 6 percent including Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, versus about 12 percent for private insurers.
anchor:
administering the Medicare program accounted for 1.4 percent of
total Medicare expenditures in 2017.

for about 6 percent of its expenditures. By comparison, private
insurers' administrative costs averaged about 12 percent in
2017.
context: CBO testimony in a House Budget Committee hearing held by the Democratic majority, 2019. The same testimony adds that coordination of care and fraud control could add administrative costs under single-payer. Different scope of "administrative" cost for Medicare (federal cost only) versus insurers (including profit).

statement: CBO projected that five illustrative single-payer options would raise federal health subsidies by $1.5 trillion to $3.0 trillion in 2030 and change total national health expenditures by between a decrease of $0.7 trillion and an increase of $0.3 trillion.
anchor: CBO projects that federal subsidies for health care would be $1.5 trillion to $3.0 trillion higher in 2030 under the illustrative single-payer options than they would be in that year under current law.
The single-payer options would change total national health expenditures (NHE) in 2030 by amounts ranging from a decrease of $0.7 trillion to an increase of $0.3 trillion.
context: CBO working paper 2020-08 and blog, December 2020 (nonpartisan, Medicare fee-for-service based; CBO did not score a specific bill). Payment rates, cost sharing and long-term care coverage drive the range; CBO says its estimates are inherently uncertain. Compare Urban (NHE up), Galvani and PERI (NHE down).

statement: CBO projected that under its single-payer options the increase in demand for health care would exceed the increase in supply, leaving more unmet demand than under current law, with delays and forgone care, particularly under lower cost sharing and lower payment rates.
anchor: The increase in demand for health care would exceed the increase in supply, resulting in more unmet demand compared with the amount under current law, CBO projects.

The increase in unmet demand would correspond to greater congestion in the health care system—including delays and forgone care—particularly under the illustrative options that include lower cost sharing and lower payment rates.
context: CBO, December 2020. Supporters argue supply would adjust and CBO also says the amount of care used would rise; RAND builds in a similar supply constraint.

statement: CBO told the Senate Budget Committee that a lower-rate scenario (hospital rates 13 percent lower, physician rates 7 percent lower, drug prices 23 percent lower) would cut national health expenditures by 9 percent and federal subsidies by 12 percent relative to a higher-rate scenario, but reduce supply by 2 percent.
anchor: In the lower-rate scenario, rates would be 13 percent lower for hospitals and 7 percent lower for physicians, on average. Also, prices for prescription drugs would be 23 percent lower, on average.
National health expenditures would be 9 percent lower.
Federal subsidies for health care would be 12 percent lower.
The supply of personal health care would be 2 percent lower, with the demand for such care roughly unchanged.
context: CBO Director Swagel, May 12, 2022, before a committee chaired by Senator Sanders. CBO had not analyzed Sanders' S. 1129. Shows that provider payment rates, not coverage, dominate cost.

statement: CBO told the Senate Budget Committee that, if a single-payer system were financed by a payroll or income tax, GDP would be approximately 1 percent to 10 percent lower by 2030 than under current law, and that all of its single-payer estimates are inherently uncertain.
anchor: Gross domestic product (GDP) would be approximately 1 percent to 10 percent lower by 2030 than the amount projected under current law
I want to emphasize that all of CBO’s estimates of the effects of a single-payer system are inherently uncertain.
context: CBO testimony, May 12, 2022. The range depends on option and tax type; supporters point out that employer and household premiums would fall, and that CBO also found non-health consumption would rise for lower-income households.

statement: Urban Institute estimated that an "enhanced" single-payer system would raise federal spending by $34.0 trillion over 10 years ($2.8 trillion in 2020) and national health spending by about $720 billion in 2020, with no one uninsured and no cost sharing.
anchor: National spending on health care would grow by about $720 billion in 2020. Federal government spending would increase by $2.8 trillion in 2020 or $34.0 trillion over 10 years.
context: Urban Institute, October 2019 (HIPSM microsimulation, 2020-2029). Enhanced design covers undocumented immigrants and adds dental, vision, hearing and long-term services, with providers paid rates closer to Medicare. Urban did not model financing.

statement: Urban Institute explained that its $34 trillion federal increase is offset by a $27 trillion decrease in spending by individuals, employers and state governments, so national health spending would rise by $7 trillion over 10 years, from $52 trillion to $59 trillion.
anchor: federal spending would increase by $34 trillion over 10 years, but health spending by individuals, employers, and state governments would decrease by $27 trillion, so national health spending would increase by $7 trillion over the same 10-year period, from $52 to $59 trillion.
context: Urban Institute blog, October 16, 2019, written to stop people comparing federal cost with national spending. Compare Galvani (13% savings) and PERI (about 10% savings), which reach the opposite sign on national spending.

statement: Urban Institute estimated that a single-payer "lite" design with income-based cost sharing and fewer new benefits would lower national health spending by $209.5 billion (6 percent) in 2020 and raise federal spending by $17.6 trillion over 10 years.
anchor: National spending on health care would decrease by $209.5 billion, or 6 percent, in 2020. Federal government spending would increase by $1.5 trillion in 2020 or $17.6 trillion over 10 years.
context: Urban Institute, October 2019. Shows design matters: the same model gives a spending rise for the enhanced design and a fall for the lite design, which leaves 10.8 million undocumented immigrants uncovered.

statement: Urban Institute estimated that a hybrid reform with improved ACA subsidies, auto-enrollment backup, a public option and capped provider payment rates would cover 25.6 million otherwise uninsured people and cut national health spending by $22.6 billion (0.6 percent) in 2020, while raising federal spending by $1.5 trillion over 10 years.
anchor: This reform plan achieves universal coverage for people legally present in the US, covering 25.6 million people who would otherwise be uninsured.

National spending on health care would decrease modestly, by $22.6 billion or 0.6 percent, compared with current law in 2020. Federal government spending would increase by $122.1 billion in 2020 or $1.5 trillion over 10 years.
context: Urban Institute, October 2019. This is a bundle (subsidies, a mandate with auto-enrollment, a public option and rate caps), not a public option alone, and it leaves 6.6 million undocumented immigrants uncovered. Cannot be read as the effect of a public option by itself.

statement: Mercatus Center estimated that the Medicare for All Act would increase federal budget commitments by about $32.6 trillion over 2022-2031, assuming provider payments more than 40 percent lower than private insurance rates.
anchor: increase federal budget commitments by approximately $32.6 trillion during its first 10 years of full implementation (2022–2031), assuming enactment in 2018
reimbursed at rates more than 40 percent lower than those currently paid by private health insurance
context: Blahous, Mercatus Center, July 2018, modeling the Sanders 2017 bill. Mercatus describes its figure as conservative because it assumes the bill's savings are achieved. A related Mercatus essay notes the same paper implied national spending about $2 trillion lower over 10 years if those assumptions held. Free-market think tank; supporters dispute it.

statement: Blahous compared his estimate with CBO's and reported that CBO's federal cost for Option 3 is $2.20 trillion lower than his lower-bound estimate, with about a quarter of the gap coming from different current-law national health expenditure baselines.
anchor: CBO’s federal cost score for Option 3 is $2.20 trillion lower than my lower-bound estimate, even though CBO uses payment rate assumptions that are slightly higher than mine.
Differences between CBO’s and my estimates of NHE under current law account for 24.9–26.5 percent of the total difference between our estimates
context: Mercatus Center brief, April 2021, by the author of the 2018 estimate; the author argues CBO's options 3 and 4 understate costs. Shows two credible estimators differing by trillions, so the cost range is wide.

statement: RAND estimated that a Medicare for All plan with long-term care benefits and no cost sharing would raise total health expenditures by 1.8 percent to $3.89 trillion in 2019, but by 9.8 percent to $4.20 trillion if there were no supply constraint.
anchor: We estimate that total health expenditures under a Medicare for All plan that provides comprehensive coverage and long-term care benefits would be $3.89 trillion in 2019 (assuming such a plan was in place for all of the year), or a 1.8 percent increase relative to expenditures under current law.
If there were no supply constraint, we estimate that total health expenditures would increase by 9.8 percent to $4.20 trillion.
context: RAND research report RR-3106, April 2019; extrapolated from earlier RAND analyses (including New York) rather than a new microsimulation. The 1.8% result depends on assuming unmet demand equals half of new demand.

statement: RAND estimated that federal health spending would rise 221 percent, from $1,090.0 billion to $3,498.7 billion in 2019 under Medicare for All, while administrative spending would fall 27.3 percent from $580.8 billion to $422.1 billion.
anchor: We estimate that federal health care spending would increase by 221 percent under Medicare for All relative to current law, from $1,090.0 billion to $3,498.7 billion.
Administrative spending falls from $580.8 billion to $422.1 billion, a reduction of 27.3 percent.
Table 1. Medicare for All: Changes in U.S. Health Care Spending, 2019 (in Billions)
context: RAND, April 2019. Administrative savings of 27.3% are smaller than PERI and Galvani assume.

statement: Galvani and colleagues calculated in The Lancet that a single-payer system would likely save 13% of national health-care expenditure, more than US$450 billion annually, and would save more than 68 000 lives a year.
anchor: we calculate that a single-payer, universal health-care system is likely to lead to a 13% savings in national health-care expenditure, equivalent to more than US$450 billion annually (based on the value of the US$ in 2017).
we estimate that ensuring health-care access for all Americans would save more than 68 000 lives and 1·73 million life-years every year compared with the status quo.
context: Lancet, Feb 15, 2020, Yale authors, funded by endowment and foundation grants (see source row). The lives-saved figure assumes uninsured mortality converges to insured mortality; the Oregon randomized trial found no detectable change in measured physical health within two years. CBO and Urban reach the opposite sign on national spending for generous designs.

statement: PERI estimated that Medicare for All could reduce total health care spending by nearly 10 percent, to $2.93 trillion, from about $3.24 trillion spent on personal health care in 2017.
anchor: As of 2017, the U.S. was spending about $3.24 trillion on personal health care
Medicare for All could reduce total health care spending in the U.S. by nearly 10 percent, to $2.93 trillion
context: Pollin et al., PERI at UMass Amherst, November 2018; authors favor the reform; modeled savings from administration, drug prices and provider fees. Mercatus and Urban reach higher national and federal costs for Sanders-type bills.

statement: EPI wrote that Pollin and colleagues' 1.8 million potentially redundant health insurance and billing administration jobs is a gross, not net, figure, and that if those workers transitioned over a four-year phase-in it would raise national layoffs by about 2% (21.5 million workers were laid off in 2018).
anchor: up to 1.8 million jobs in the health insurance and billing administration sector

If the 1.8 million workers that Pollin et al. (2018) identify as potentially being displaced by M4A were forced to transition over the four-year phase-in commonly identified with M4A plans, this would increase the national rate of layoffs by about 2%.
21.5 million workers were laid off in 2018
context: Economic Policy Institute, March 2020, a labor-aligned think tank sympathetic to the reform; it does say policymakers should support displaced workers. The 1.8 million figure includes administrative staff at hospitals and physician offices, not only insurers.

statement: BLS counted 601.8 thousand jobs in direct health and medical insurance carriers in 2025 and projected 622.6 thousand in 2035.
anchor: Employment by industry, occupation, and percent distribution, 2025 and projected 2035 .

Total, all occupations
00-0000
Summary
601.8
100.0
0.4
622.6
context: BLS Employment Projections matrix, industry 524114; official data and baseline projection with no policy change. Counts the insurance carriers only; billing and administration staff in provider offices are in other industries.

statement: A systematic review of 22 single-payer cost analyses found that 19 (86%) predicted net savings in the first year (median 3.46% of total costs), but it also excluded two widely publicized studies that found net costs.
anchor: Our search yielded economic analyses of the cost of 22 single-payer plans over the past 30 years.
We found that 19 (86%) of the analyses predicted net savings (median net result was a savings of 3.46% of total costs) in the first year of program operation

we excluded 2 widely publicized studies [20, 24], both of which found net costs, on the grounds that these studies made assumptions that included private insurance intermediaries (i.e., not a single-payer) or lacked technical detail for evaluation.
context: Cai et al., PLOS Medicine, January 2020 (UC authors; peer reviewed). The review says the studies were too heterogeneous for formal meta-analysis; net cost or savings in year one ranged from +7.2% to -15.5%. It measures national spending, not federal cost, and so does not contradict Urban's federal increase.

statement: Washington's own Health Care Authority reported that in 2025 its Cascade Select public option silver plans were the lowest-premium qualified health plans in 26 of 39 counties (down from 31 in 2024), and that public option premiums were meaningfully lower than non-public option premiums in zero counties.
anchor: 2025 Public Option Progress Snapshot
Public option silver plans are lowest-premium QHPs in 26 of 39 counties, down from 31 counties in 2024.
Public option premiums in zero counties are “meaningfully lower” than non-public option premiums.
context: Washington State Health Care Authority slide deck, 2025 progress snapshot; self-report by the agency that runs the program, candid about a shortfall. The same deck says the program is the fastest-growing plan for a second year and that the 160% of Medicare aggregate provider reimbursement cap is the main lever.

statement: Washington's Cascade Care law capped aggregate provider reimbursement in Cascade Select plans at 160% of Medicare; Cascade Select launched in 2021, and every hospital is required to contract with at least one Cascade Select plan.
anchor: Capped aggregate provider reimbursement at 160% of Medicare
Cascade Select launched in 2021
Every hospital is required to contract with at least one Cascade Select plan
context: Washington Health Care Authority summary of RCW 41.05.405 and SB 5377 (2021). Statutory design: a cap on aggregate rates, not a fee schedule, and a hospital participation rule.

statement: Washington's exchange reported that 94,000 customers were in a Cascade Select public option plan, up 50% from 2024, out of 309,000 customers who selected qualified health plans.
anchor: 309,000 customers selected QHPs.
94,000 customers are in a Cascade Select public option plan, up 50% from 2024.
context: Washington Health Benefit Exchange open enrollment preview, March 13, 2025; administrative counts. Mathematica notes the public option captured only about 1 percent of exchange enrollment in its first year (2021).

statement: Washington's Health Care Authority proposed legislation to set a hospital-specific rate cap at 135% of Medicare for public option plans and tie state subsidies to public option enrollment, noting over 115,000 enrollees as of February 2026.
anchor: Adjust reference pricing structure to incorporate a hospital-specific rate cap at 135% of Medicare, excluding children’s hospitals and certain other small or rural hospitals.
over 115,000 enrollees selecting plans as of February 2026
context: Washington Health Care Authority proposal, 2026 (agency request; not law). It signals that the state judges the 160% aggregate cap too loose to produce meaningfully lower premiums.

statement: Colorado's Division of Insurance reported that 132,791 people enrolled in the Colorado Option in 2025 open enrollment, 47% of selections on Connect for Health Colorado, up from 13.7% in 2023 and 34% in 2024.
anchor: 132,791 people enrolling in the Colorado Option during the open enrollment period that just concluded, representing 47% of all selections for 2025 on Connect for Health Colorado.
In its first year, 2023, Colorado Option enrollment made up 13.7% of selections on Connect for Health. In 2024, that share jumped to 34%
context: Colorado Division of Insurance press release, January 23, 2025, issued with the Governor; administrative counts but promotional framing. Mathematica (for the same agency) gives the same 47% figure.

statement: The Colorado Option law set premium rate reduction targets of at least 5 percent for 2023, 10 percent for 2024 and 15 percent for 2025 relative to 2021 premiums in the same county, adjusted for medical inflation, with a 20% reimbursement rate reduction target negotiated through public hearings.
anchor: 2023 PRR Target: At least a 5-percent reduction in premiums relative to the premiums offered by the carrier in the same county in 2021, adjusted for medical inflation
2024 PRR Target: At least a 10-percent reduction in premiums relative to the premiums offered by the carrier in the same county in 2021, adjusted for medical inflation
2025 PRR Target: At least a 15-percent reduction in premiums relative to the premiums offered by the carrier in the same county in 2021, adjusted for medical inflation
Reimbursement Rate Reduction Target (through public hearing process): 20% from Plan Year 2024 negotiated rate
context: Mathematica report for the Colorado Division of Insurance (date approximate); the targets are statutory (C.R.S. 10-16-1304). The same report reports 15 percent lower out-of-pocket spending for enrollees but only carrier-reported premium reductions, and that settlements were negotiated rather than litigated.

statement: The Colorado Association of Health Plans reported that hospitals said Colorado hospitals expected to lose $125 million this year because of what they characterize as inadequate reimbursements, and that a Brown University Health Affairs study found the Colorado Option reduced the average marketplace premium by $101 a month compared with 2020.
anchor: Colorado hospitals expect to lose $125 million this year due to what they characterize as inadequate reimbursements, according to the provider group.
The Colorado Option has reduced the average marketplace premium by $101 a month compared with 2020, according to a Brown University study published in the journal Health Affairs on Jan. 15.
context: Colorado Association of Health Plans (insurer trade group), January 29, 2025, relaying the hospital association's loss estimate and the Brown/Health Affairs finding. The $125 million is a hospital-industry claim, not independently verified; the Brown study itself was not read here.

statement: KFF Health News reported that 10,762 people enrolled in Nevada's Battle Born State Plans in the first open enrollment, under a third of the roughly 35,000 state officials had projected, among 104,000 marketplace purchasers.
anchor: State officials projected ahead of open enrollment that about 35,000 people would purchase the public option plans. Of the 104,000 people who had purchased a plan on the state marketplace as of mid-January, 10,762 had enrolled in one of the public option plans
less than a third of what state officials had projected
context: KFF Health News, Feb 19, 2026. Nevada officials say the projection predated a 26% average individual-market rate increase and loss of enhanced subsidies. Nevada law requires 15% premium reductions over four years against a benchmark silver plan.

statement: United States of Care reported that in plan year 2026 the average gross premium for Nevada's Battle Born State Plans was approximately 4.7% lower, and non-public option marketplace plans were about 4.6% lower than they would have been without the public option.
anchor: in plan year 2026 (the first plan year in which Nevada’s public option was available), the average total (gross) premium for Battle Born State Plans was approximately 4.7% lower
non-public option Marketplace plans – which are about 4.6% lower in 2026 than they would have been without the public option
context: United States of Care issue brief (an advocacy group favoring public options), September 2026; counterfactual claim of 4.6% is an estimate whose method was not checked. Same brief says Colorado Option plans save $14 to $33 per month in 2026.

statement: Vermont's Green Mountain Care financing report, submitted by Governor Shumlin on December 30, 2014, estimated an 11.5 percent payroll tax on employers plus an income-based public premium rising to 9.5 percent of income, capped at $27,500, to replace private premiums.
anchor: We estimated the payroll tax at 11.5 percent for the preferred policy choices we are including in this report. Additionally, to fully fund GMC, the highest-income Vermonters would pay 9.5 percent of income through a public premium, up to a maximum of $27,500
Submitted by Governor Peter Shumlin to the Vermont State Legislature December 30, 2014
locator: Executive summary and chapter on taxes
context: State of Vermont report, Dec 30, 2014 (the administration of a single-payer supporter). It is the state's own financing estimate, and the governor then declined to pursue the plan. Taxes would replace employer and household premiums, so net burden is lower than the gross rates suggest; the report also did not cost the small-business transition.

statement: VTDigger reported that Governor Shumlin would not pursue single payer after modeling showed the price tag was $2.6 billion, not the $1.6 billion to $2.2 billion originally believed.
anchor: The price tag for a publicly financed universal health care system turned out to be $2.6 billion, not the $1.6 billion to $2.2 billion that Shumlin and his team originally believed.
context: VTDigger news report, Dec 17, 2014. Journalistic account of a government announcement; the $2.6 billion is the administration's figure. Vermont is a small state with a 94% actuarial value benefit and limited ability to raise tax without cross-border effects.

statement: Healthcare Finance News reported that the Green Mountain Care Board considered the "hundreds of millions of dollars" in predicted administrative savings "not practical to achieve" and that expected federal waiver funding was now less than half of the $267 million first expected.
anchor: The "hundreds of millions of dollars" in administrative savings that were predicted are now considered by the Green Mountain Care Board "not practical to achieve."
less than half of the $267 million initially expected
context: Healthcare Finance News (trade publication), December 18, 2014. Shows what went wrong in Vermont: admin savings and federal funding came in below assumption. Supporters of single payer say Vermont could not use federal Medicare and ERISA dollars and was too small.

statement: California's Senate Appropriations staff estimated SB 562 (2017) would cost about $400 billion per year, with about $200 billion in existing funding and about $200 billion in new tax revenue needed, roughly a 15% payroll tax if raised that way.
anchor: SB 562 would create a universal, single-payer health care system in California.
Version: April 17, 2017
Total annual costs of about $400 billion per year, including all covered health care services and administrative costs, at full enrollment.

About $200 billion in additional tax revenues would be needed to pay for the remainder of the total program cost. Assuming that this cost was raised through a new payroll tax (with no cap on wages subject to the tax), the additional payroll tax rate would be about 15% of earned income.
context: Senate Appropriations Committee staff fiscal summary, May 22, 2017, for SB 562 by Senator Lara. It warns estimates are "subject to enormous uncertainty" and notes employers and employees already spend $100 to $150 billion on coverage, so new spending would be $50 to $100 billion. PERI's competing estimate was $331 billion.

statement: CHBRP reported that PERI estimated SB 562 would cost $331 billion as of 2017 and cut overall costs by about 18%, versus the Senate Appropriations Committee's estimate of about $400 billion.
anchor: The Senate Committee on Appropriations analysis predicted total annual costs of about $400 billion per year

The authors (Pollin, et al., 2017) estimated that through implementation of Healthy California (SB 562), overall costs of providing full health care coverage to all Californians could fall by about 18% relative to spending levels under the existing system.
PERI, on the other hand, estimated, "The overall annual costs of this single-payer system for California would be $331 billion as of 2017,"
context: California Health Benefits Review Program (University of California, legislature-mandated), April 2021; reports both estimates. PERI authors favor single payer; Appropriations staff are nonpartisan. The two differ in how much spending on administration, drug prices and provider fees falls.

statement: AB 1400, California's single-payer bill, died in January 2022 without a floor vote after its author concluded it lacked the votes; it did not say how the system would be paid for, and an analysis estimated California would spend about $517 billion on health care in 2022.
anchor: It became clear that we did not have the votes necessary for passage, and I decided the best course of action is to not put AB 1400 for a vote today,
California is on pace to spend about $517 billion on health care in 2022, according to an analysis by a commission established by Gov. Gavin Newsom to study universal health care.
context: Associated Press story on NPR, Jan 31, 2022. Reports business and insurance industry pressure and that debate was dominated by cost. The $517 billion is from the Healthy California for All Commission.

statement: Uwe Reinhardt wrote in the BMJ that overnight health insurance coverage in Taiwan jumped from roughly 57% of the population before 1 March 1995 to virtually the entire population, and that the insurance bureau's administrative budget was 1.5% of total spending.
anchor: Overnight, health insurance coverage in Taiwan jumped from roughly 57% of the population before 1 March 1995 to virtually the entire population.
the Bureau of National Health Insurance, which now accounts for only an inadequate 1.5% of total spending on the health insurance system
context: BMJ, Jan 2008, by Uwe Reinhardt (Princeton economist, a single-payer sympathizer). It also finds Taiwan underfunds its system by perhaps 1-2% of GDP; see the next entry. Taiwan's system is a mostly tax-and-premium financed model with a small, rich-by-assumption administrative budget.

statement: The same BMJ article said Taiwan could much improve its health system by allocating an additional 1-2% of GDP to health care and that patients' own spending was still higher than in most European nations.
anchor: Taiwan could much improve its health system by allocating an additional, say, 1-2% of its gross domestic product to health care.
Some of the additional funds could be used to reduce patients' own spending, which is still higher than that in most European nations.
context: Same source as above; a qualification from a supporter. Low administrative cost and low spending are partly a result of tight global budgets and underfunding.

statement: Cheng wrote that by the end of 1995, 90 percent of Taiwan's then 21 million residents were enrolled, and that NHI administrative cost was 0.87 percent of total NHI expenditure in 2018.
anchor: by the end of 1995, 90 percent of Taiwan’s then 21 million residents were enrolled.
NHI’s administrative cost accounted for 0.87 percent of the total NHI expenditure in 2018.
context: Milken Institute Review, May 2020, by Tsung-mei Cheng (who favors the Taiwan model). Administrative share uses NHI expenditure as denominator; compare Reinhardt's 1.5% and the journal overview's "under 2%".

statement: The Fraser Institute's 2024 survey found physicians reported a median wait of 30.0 weeks from GP referral to treatment in Canada, up from 27.7 weeks in 2023, based on 1,973 responses and a 17.0% response rate.
anchor: In 2024, physicians across Canada reported a median wait time of 30.0 weeks between a referral from a GP and receipt of treatment. Up from 27.7 in 2023.
A total of 1,973 responses were received across the 12 specialties surveyed—a response rate of 17.0%.
context: Fraser Institute, December 2024 (market-oriented think tank, critic of Canada's single-payer model). The survey takes the median of specialist physicians' self-reported waits for elective care; the report itself warns of low responses in some provinces. Government data (CIHI) measure benchmark attainment instead.

statement: CIHI reported that in 2024, 68% of hip replacements and 61% of knee replacements in Canada were done within the recommended 6 months and 69% of cataract surgeries within 112 days, all below 2019 levels for hip and knee.
anchor: In 2024, compared with previous years, more patients across Canada received hip (68%) and knee (61%) replacements within the recommended 6 months and cataract surgeries (69%) within the recommended 112 days. However, for hip and knee replacements, these percentages remain below 2019 (pre–COVID-19 pandemic) levels.
context: Canadian Institute for Health Information, June 12, 2025; official data from provincial systems, with differing provincial reporting definitions. Shows long waits for some elective procedures in a single-payer system, but also 26% more hip replacements than in 2019.

statement: The Commonwealth Fund reported that Switzerland (since 1996) and the Netherlands (since 2006) reach universal coverage through an individual mandate to buy private basic insurance, with uninsured rates of about 1.5 percent and below 1 percent, about 40 percent of residents receiving premium assistance, and risk equalization among insurers.
anchor: the individual mandate in the Netherlands took effect in 2006
uninsured rates are low (estimated at about 1.5 percent of the population in the Netherlands and below 1 percent in Switzerland)
Both countries subsidize premiums for low-income households, with about 40 percent receiving such premium assistance.
The Swiss have operated with a mandate since 1996.
context: Commonwealth Fund report, 2009 (a foundation favoring universal coverage); data are 15 years old and both systems have since changed. Both require open enrollment, community rating and risk equalization, which a U.S. market-based reform would also need.

statement: The Commonwealth Fund's Germany profile reported that health insurance has been mandatory since 2007, about 86 percent of the population is in statutory competing nonprofit sickness funds, funds are paid by a risk-adjusted capitation formula, and higher earners can opt out to private insurance.
anchor: Approximately 86 percent of the population is en-rolled in statutory health insurance
A risk-adjusted capitation formula is used, accounting for age, sex, and morbidity from 80 chronic and serious illnesses.
The final step toward universal health coverage occurred in 2007
context: Commonwealth Fund International Health Care System Profiles (2020 edition; figures c. 2019). Germany combines mandate, regulated competing funds, a central health fund and an opt-out for higher earners; the page text has a hyphenation artifact "en-rolled".

statement: The Commonwealth Fund reported that Australia's Medicare covers 100% of the population, that about half of Australians also buy private supplementary insurance, and that the government pays a rebate toward premiums and charges a tax penalty on higher-income households that do not purchase private insurance.
anchor: Approximately half of Australians buy private supplementary insurance to pay for private hospital care, dental services, and other services. The federal government pays a rebate toward this premium and also charges a tax penalty on higher-income households that do not take up private insurance.
Public coverage: 100%
context: Commonwealth Fund overview, December 2020; the 46% (private hospital) and 55% (general treatment) figures appear in the same page. A newer 2026 Commonwealth Fund Australia page exists that was read only in part (it lists 55% private insurance coverage).

statement: The Commonwealth Fund's Mirror, Mirror 2024 ranked Australia, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom as the top three of 10 countries and the United States last overall, while the U.S. ranked second on care process.
anchor: Goal: Compare health system performance in 10 countries, including the United States
The United States ranks last overall (Exhibits 1 and 2). The three top-performing countries in 2024 are Australia, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom.
even the U.S., with the lowest-ranked health system, ranks second in the care process domain.
context: Commonwealth Fund, Sept 2024 (70 measures, five domains, 10 countries). The report cautions that differences between most countries are small and every country has weaknesses. The Fund advocates coverage expansion. Top-three include a multi-payer system (Netherlands), a tax-financed public system (UK) and a hybrid (Australia), so the ranking does not favor one design.

statement: CMS's evaluation of the Maryland All-Payer Model (2014-2018) found total Medicare expenditures declined by 2.8% and hospital expenditures by 4.1%, driven by a 17.2% reduction in outpatient department expenditures, and commercial hospital expenditure growth was 6.1% slower.
anchor: Final Evaluation Report (2014-2018)

Total Medicare expenditures
declined by 2.8% and hospital
expenditures declined by 4.1%
A 17.2% reduction in outpatient
Commercial insurance had 6.1% slower growth in total hospital
context: CMS Innovation Center summary of an independent RTI evaluation (publication year approximate). CMS also reports that growth in total commercial expenditures did not slow. Maryland sets uniform all-payer hospital rates and a global budget, which resembles the price-setting part of any single-payer or public option design.

statement: CMS reported that the Maryland Total Cost of Care Model reduced Medicare fee-for-service spending by 2.1% and hospital admissions by 16.2% during 2019–2022, reduced total Medicare spending by $689 million from 2019 to 2021, and that its primary care program cost CMS about $96 million annually without significant offsetting savings.
anchor: Evaluation of the First Four Years (2019–2022)

During the MD TCOC period, the model reduced Medicare fee-for-service spending by 2.1%, reduced hospital
admissions by 16.2%, and reduced disparities in several quality measures. From 2019 to 2021, the model reduced
total Medicare spending—including non-claims payments—by $689 million.
MDPCP cost CMS about $96 million
context: CMS Innovation Center summary of Mathematica evaluation, 2024; effects of all changes since 2014 combined, and the summary notes effects on total spending have gotten smaller since 2019. Savings accrue to Medicare, not to commercial payers.

statement: CMS noted that Maryland committed to $2 billion in Medicare savings over 8 years under its Total Cost of Care Model, and that the model increased non-hospital spending substantially in 2021, lessening total Medicare savings that year.
anchor:
committing to $2 billion in
Medicare savings over 8 years

However, the Model increased non-hospital spending substantially in 2021, lessening overall Medicare
savings that year.
context: CMS Innovation Center summary of Mathematica's three-year evaluation, 2022. Cuts hospital spending but total savings can be eroded as spending shifts outside the hospital global budget.

statement: A Health Affairs difference-in-differences study estimated that Oregon's October 2019 hospital payment cap for its state employee plan saved $107.5 million (4 percent of plan spending) in the first two years, though inpatient facility prices fell significantly only in the second year.
anchor: We estimated $107.5 million (or 4 percent of total plan spending) in savings to the state employee plan during the first two years.
In October 2019, the Oregon state employee health insurance plan instituted a cap on hospital payments.
was associated with a significant reduction in the second year after implementation (−$2,774.20)
context: Murray, Brown, Miller, Norton and Ryan, Health Affairs, March 2024; peer reviewed, Oregon All Payer All Claims 2014-21. The cap is 200% of Medicare in network; the study finds no significant inpatient price reduction across the whole post period.

statement: Health Affairs commentary reported that Oregon's cap at 200 percent of Medicare saves the state around $50 million annually, all 24 network hospitals stayed in network, and the policy did not raise prices in the non-state employee commercial market; Washington has since become the second state to adopt a similar cap.
anchor: cap the amount that the state’s employee health plan would pay hospitals at 200 percent of Medicare rates for in-network services and 185 percent for out-of-network services.
saving the state of Oregon around $50 million annually since its implementation. To date, all 24 hospitals that were in the plan’s network prior to the policy have remained in-network
This policy did not lead to higher prices among the non-state employee commercial market.
the State of Washington joined Oregon to become the second state to adopt an across-the-board cap on hospital payments
context: Health Affairs Forefront commentary (Hostert), Oct 2025; not peer reviewed, summarizing studies. Policy is a cap for state employee plans only, not all-payer.

statement: A Health Affairs simulation estimated that payment caps at 200 percent of Medicare would have saved state employee plans an average of $150.2 million per state in 2022 ($7.1 billion nationally) while commercial hospital operating margins would fall from an average of 42.7 percent to 41.7 percent.
anchor: payment caps set at 200 percent of Medicare rates would have saved state employee plans an average of $150.2 million per state in 2022 (0.35 percent of state expenditures), leading to aggregate savings of $7.1 billion nationally. Commercial hospital operating margins would remain healthy under this cap, falling from an average of 42.7 percent to 41.7 percent.
