Most of these appropriations must be liquidated by the end of FY2023 (September 30). Only the ARPA
CCDBG funds may remain available for expenditure for another year
context: CRS (nonpartisan) on enacted appropriations.

statement: HHS's May 2026 final rule, effective July 13, 2026, rescinds the Biden administration's CCDF rule's requirements to cap family copayments at 7 percent of income, to fund some care through grants or contracts, to pay providers prospectively and to pay them by enrollment; states may keep those policies.
anchor: It rescinds the requirements to limit family co-payments to 7 percent of family income, to provide some direct services through grants or contracts, to pay providers prospectively, and to pay providers based on enrollment.
Effective: July 13, 2026.
context: Second Trump administration; the rule is primary law (data). Its stated rationale (state waivers, cost) is the administration's view. The 2024 rule was a Biden administration rule.

statement: HHS reports that in FY2023, CCDF subsidized more than 1.6 million children from 994,000 families each month, and that FY2026 enacted CCDF funding is $12.381 billion.
anchor: Federal Fiscal year (FFY) 2026 enacted CCDF funding is $12.381 billion awarded by formula to States, Territories, and Tribes.
In FFY 2023, the most recent year for which data is available, CCDF provided subsidies to more than 1.6 million children from 994,000 families each month.
context: Administrative counts in the rule's background, second Trump administration.

statement: In FY2024 Head Start (including Early Head Start) was funded to serve 715,873 children and pregnant women.
anchor: In fiscal year (FY) 2024, the Head Start program was funded to serve 715,873 children, pregnant women, in centers, family homes, and family child care homes.
context: Federal program data; the FY2025 edition was not found.

statement: On July 14, 2025 HHS reinterpreted "federal public benefit" under the 1996 welfare law (PRWORA) to include Head Start, which would bar many immigrant children; a federal court enjoined it, and on December 15, 2025 the appeals court granted the government's motion to drop its appeal.
anchor: on July 14, 2025, HHS issued a directive reinterpreting the phrase 'federal public benefit' in the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA) to include Head Start effective immediately
On December 4, 2025, the Defendants filed a motion to voluntarily dismiss their appeal, which the appellate court granted on December 15.
context: A law school's summary of court records (W.D. Wash.; preliminary injunction September 2025). A separate injunction (D.R.I.) covers plaintiff states. The case continued as of September 2026; this register does not hold the orders themselves.

statement: In 2022 families spent 8.9% to 16.0% of median family income on full-day care for one child, with annual prices of $6,552 to $15,600 (National Database of Childcare Prices).
anchor: U.S. families spend between 8.9% and 16.0% of their median income on full-day care for just one child, with annual prices ranging from $6,552 to $15,600 in 2022, the most recent year for which data are available.

statement: Child Care Aware of America finds the national average annual price of child care was $13,184 in 2025.
anchor: CCAoA found that the national average annual price of child care in 2025 was $13,184.
context: Child care advocacy organization with a stake in showing high prices; state-reported data, averaged by its own method ($12,609 to $13,644 by method). Consistent with the DOL database's range (EV-CAR-514).

statement: The median hourly wage for childcare workers was $16.82 in May 2025, and there were 1,010,300 childcare worker jobs in 2025 (including the self-employed).
anchor: The median hourly wage for childcare workers was $16.82 in May 2025.
Number of Jobs, 2025 | 1,010,300
context: BLS OEWS and employment projections. About $34,980 a year at full time (project arithmetic, 2,080 hours).

statement: The median annual wage for preschool teachers was $38,140 in May 2025, with 583,200 jobs in 2025.
anchor: The median annual wage for preschool teachers was $38,140 in May 2025.
Number of Jobs, 2025 | 583,200
context: BLS. Preschool teachers include public-school pre-K teachers, who are paid more (EV-CAR-521).

statement: In 2025 the labor force participation rate of women with own children under 6 was 68.0 percent (68.3 percent a year earlier), against 95.3 percent for men.
anchor: WITH OWN CHILDREN UNDER 6 YEARS
context: BLS CPS; columns are 2024 total, men, women, then 2025 total, men, women. 2025 averages omit October 2025.

statement: In the 2024-2025 school year state-funded preschool enrolled nearly 1.8 million children, 37% of 4-year-olds and 9% of 3-year-olds; states spent nearly $14.4 billion, about $8,124 per child.
anchor: Nationally, enrollment reached nearly 1.8 million children during the 2024-2025 school year, including 37% of 4-year-olds and 9% of 3-year-olds.
states invested nearly $14.4 billion, or an average of $8,124 per child enrolled.
locator: Executive summary, "Historic and Emerging Preschool Leaders"; yearbook landing page
context: NIEER, a pre-K research and advocacy institute; the data are state-reported and compiled consistently over 23 years. State spending only (federal Head Start excluded).

statement: The Census Bureau estimates the U.S. population at 341,784,857 on July 1, 2025, with 5.4% under 5 years old
anchor: Persons under 5 years, percent | 5.4%
Population estimates, July 1, 2025, (V2025) | 341,784,857
context: Census estimates; the 18.5 million is project arithmetic (5.4% of the total).

statement: Markowitz and Bassok report early educators' median salaries are highest in school-based public pre-K ($53,200 in 2022), then Head Start ($35,819) and child care ($29,570).
anchor: salaries are highest in school-based public pre-k ($53,200 in 2022), followed by Head Start ($35,819), and child care ($29,570, both home- and center-based)
context: Academic review (UVA); secondary compilation of survey data. Supports the pay gap that drives the under-3 staffing critique; it does not measure staff moving from infant care to pre-K.

statement: Baker, Gruber and Milligan find Quebec's low-fee universal child care raised mothers' labor supply (an elasticity of 0.236) but left children worse off on behavior and health, from aggression to motor-social skills to illness.
anchor: The labor supply impact is highly significant, and our measured elasticity of 0.236 is slightly smaller than previous credible estimates. Finally, we uncover striking evidence that children are worse off in a variety of behavioral and health dimensions, ranging from aggression to motor-social skills to illness.
context: Quasi-experimental (difference-in-differences) peer-reviewed economics; the authors are not advocates for or against the program. Quality and the care children would otherwise have had shape the sign (compare Norway, EV-CAR-543).

statement: Baker, Gruber and Milligan find the negative effects of Quebec's program on noncognitive outcomes persisted, and exposed cohorts had worse health, lower life satisfaction and higher crime: accusations rose 353 per 100,000 against a mean of 1,872, about 19 percent.
anchor: We find that the negative effects on noncognitive outcomes persisted to school ages, and also that cohorts with increased child care access had worse health, lower life satisfaction, and higher crime rates later in life.
For accused across all categories, we estimate a rise of 353 per 100,000 children, compared to a mean of 1,872 accusations. This is a rise of 19 percent.
context: Same research team as EV-CAR-530; finds no lasting effect on cognitive scores. Province-level cohorts, so other Quebec changes could confound. Independent qualification: Haeck, Lefebvre and Merrigan (EV-CAR-535) find the harms do not show for teens in their data.

statement: Lefebvre and Merrigan find Quebec's child care policy had a large and statistically significant effect on the labor supply of mothers with preschool children.
anchor: the results show that the policy had a large and statistically significant impact on the labor supply of mothers with preschool children.
context: Quasi-experimental, independent of Baker, Gruber and Milligan; Quebec economists.

statement: Fortin, Godbout and St-Cerny estimate that in 2008 Quebec's low-fee child care led nearly 70,000 more mothers to hold jobs (3.8% more women employed) and raised Quebec's GDP by about 1.7% ($5 billion).
anchor: in 2008 universal access to low-fee childcare in Quebec induced nearly 70,000 more mothers to hold jobs than if no such program had existed - an increase of 3.8% in women employment. By our calculation, Quebec's domestic income (GDP) was higher by about 1.7% ($5 billion) as a result.
context: Simulation by Quebec public-finance economists who argue the program pays for itself; the employment effect rests on earlier studies. Contested: Haeck, Lefebvre and Merrigan (2015) find the costs exceed the provincial fiscal return (reported via the Fraser Institute, not in the register); Baker, Gruber and Milligan (2026, EV-CAR-534) find 75-117 percent recaptured.

statement: Baker, Gruber and Milligan (2026) estimate the net present value of the fiscal benefits of Quebec's program may recapture between 75 and 117 percent of its upfront costs, through mothers' higher lifetime employment and earnings.
anchor: the net present value of the flow of fiscal benefits may recapture between 75 and 117 percent of the upfront costs of the program.
context: NBER working paper (not yet peer-reviewed); same team that found child harms (EV-CAR-530, 531), so not a team inclined to favor the program. Independent of Fortin and others (EV-CAR-533), which it qualifies.

statement: Haeck, Lefebvre and Merrigan find that ten years on, Quebec's reform did not improve school readiness and may have harmed children from low-income families, while mothers' participation rose durably.
anchor: our results on cognitive development suggest the reform did not improve school readiness and may even have had negative impacts on children from low-income families.
context: Quasi-experimental, independent of Baker, Gruber and Milligan. A later paper by Haeck and others (2018) finds the harms do not persist for teens 12-19.

statement: Quebec's 2003 quality survey found 53% of preschool-age children in nonprofit centres (CPEs) received care of only fair quality and 42% good or very good; for-profit centres rated lower.
anchor: slightly more than half of children in the preschool age category (53%) were receiving daycare services judged to be of Fair quality, while 42% were receiving Good or Very Good educational daycare.
context: Official Quebec survey; for-profit centres scored about 2.6 of 4 against 2.93 for CPEs (ISQ's private-daycare brochure, not in the register). The 2014 survey renamed "fair" as "acceptable".

statement: Canada's Budget 2021 committed up to $27.2 billion over five years from 2021-22 to a Canada-wide early learning and child care system.
anchor: Budget 2021 proposes to invest up to $27.2 billion over five years, starting in 2021-22 as part of initial 5-year agreements.
context: Government of Canada (Liberal government). Canadian dollars. Later stated as about $30 billion with Indigenous child care.

statement: Canada's Auditor General found that by March 2024 provinces and territories had cut average fees in federally funded spaces to about $16.50 a day, against a $10 target for March 2026, which 5 provinces and 3 territories had met.
anchor: as of March 2024, provincial and territorial governments reduced the average out-of-pocket fees for regulated child care spaces that received federal funding to approximately $16.50 per day across Canada. The target is to reach an average of $10 per day by March 2026. As of March 2024, 5 provinces and 3 territories had already met this target.
context: Independent auditor (Office of the Auditor General). It also found about 112,000 new spaces after three years, against a 250,000 target by 2026.

statement: C.D. Howe reports that the share of Canadian children under six on a child care waitlist rose from 19.1 percent in 2022 to 30.8 percent in 2025 among children not in care, and from 16.7 to 23.6 percent among those already in care.
anchor: Nationally, the share of children under age six who were on a waitlist rose from 19.1 percent in 2022 to 30.8 percent in 2025 among children not in childcare, and from 16.7 percent to 23.6 percent among those already using childcare.
context: A critic's use of Statistics Canada survey data; it also cautions that waitlists overstate demand (children are on many lists).

statement: Canada's Parliamentary Budget Officer projected that in 2026 the budgeted money would subsidize 678,800 full-time spaces, 182,000 fewer than the estimated demand.
anchor: PBO projected that in 2026, with 90% of gross funding allocated to subsidies, the 2021 budgeted funding would subsidize 678,800 full-time equivalent spaces, which is 182,000 fewer slots than required to meet the estimated demand at that time.
context: Independent budget office projection. Supported by the later waitlist data (EV-CAR-539) and the Auditor General's space count (EV-CAR-538).

statement: Havnes and Mogstad find Norway's subsidized child care expansion had strong positive effects on children's educational attainment and labor market participation and reduced welfare dependency.
anchor: Our precise and robust difference-in-differences estimates show that subsidized child care had strong positive effects on children's educational attainment and labor market participation, and also reduced welfare dependency.
context: Quasi-experimental, independent of the Quebec studies; Norwegian public, regulated, mostly high-quality kindergartens in the 1970s. Contrasts with Quebec (EV-CAR-530, 531).

statement: Havnes and Mogstad find Norway's .1785 increase in child care coverage (as a share of children) caused less than a 1 percentage point rise in maternal employment, mostly replacing informal care.
anchor: The .1785 increase in child care coverage is estimated to have caused less than 1 percentage point increase in maternal employment.
context: Same authors as EV-CAR-543. Contests the Quebec employment results (EV-CAR-530, 532): employment gains depend on how many mothers already work and on informal care.

statement: The OECD reports total education spending on 3-5-year-olds averages 0.59% of GDP across OECD countries, highest in Iceland (1.05%), Norway (0.87%), Israel (0.85%) and Sweden (0.82%).
anchor: total education expenditure on 3-5 year-olds averages 0.59% of GDP across OECD countries, with the highest shares in Iceland (1.05% of GDP), Norway (0.87%), Israel (0.85%) and Sweden (0.82%)
context: OECD official statistics; covers educational programs for ages 3-5, not all child care. A separate OECD measure puts all public ECEC at 0.8% of GDP on average in 2021 and 1.7% in Norway.

statement: New Mexico's Legislative Finance Committee estimates that if universal assistance drew 90 percent of privately paid slots, the program's cost would almost double to $849.7 million a year.
anchor: LFC estimates that if universal assistance include 90 percent uptake of all available slots in the state currently paying privately, the cost of Childcare Assistance to taxpayers would almost double to $849.7 million annually
context: Legislative fiscal staff, independent of the agency running the program (ECECD), whose own brief projects $445.8 million in FY2026 rising to $728.1 million in FY2029 (not in the register). The two disagree on take-up; no outcome evaluation exists yet.

statement: Urban Institute estimates New Mexico's rule changes between October 2019 and May 2022, raised the number of children eligible for subsidies by 70 percent.
anchor: changes to the rules between October 2019 and May 2022 increased the number of New Mexico children eligible for CCDF by 70 percent and increased the number of families eligible for CCDF by 71 percent
context: Microsimulation of eligibility, not of use. The University of New Mexico's data show children served rose about 39 percent (19,366 to 26,941) while license-exempt home providers fell 38 percent (not in the register).

statement: Washington's 2025 budget law delays the Working Connections Child Care expansion from 60 to 75 percent of state median income from July 2025 to July 2029, and to 85 percent from 2027 to 2031.
anchor: Delays the Working Connections Child Care (WCCC) Program eligibility expansion from 60 to 75 percent of State Median Income (SMI) from July 1, 2025, to July 1, 2029, and delays the eligibility expansion from 75 to 85 percent of SMI from July 1, 2027, to July 1, 2031.
context: State law (legislative staff summary). The 2021 Fair Start for Kids Act had capped copayments at 7 percent of income; a 2026 DCYF page says the expansion is now canceled and eligibility stays at 60 percent (not verified against a bill).

statement: Urban Institute's evaluation finds DC child care centers that took subsidies and joined the pay equity fund had 37 percent educator turnover, against 51 percent at subsidy-serving centers without the wage increases. The fund's FY2025 minimum salaries ran from about $51,000 to $75,000, against an average of about $37,300 for DC child care workers before it.
anchor: Centers that accepted children with subsidies and participated in the fund had a turnover rate that matched the District average (37 percent), but turnover jumped to 51 percent in centers that did not offer wage enhancements and accepted children with subsidies.
minimum annual salaries range from about $51,000
to $75,000 (for lead teachers with a bachelor's degree)
compares with an average of about $37,300 for all workers employed in DC child care in May 2021, before the fund's implementation
context: Program evaluation on administrative data; participation was voluntary, so selection may explain part of the gap. The fund was cut 20 percent in FY2025, minimum salaries lowered 4-5 percent from January 2026, and the mayor proposed ending it for FY2027 (Urban and OSSE, not in the register). Supports the wage-retention link with the Military Child Care system (EV-CAR-551).

statement: RAND finds the Military Child Care Act required at least 50 military child development centers to become accredited, a provision that alone led to significant quality improvements; the Act also set fees by family income and DoD tied pay rises to training.
anchor: As a means of promoting excellence and professionalism, the act called for at least 50 military CDCs to become accredited. This provision alone led to significant quality improvements
context: RAND program evaluation for DoD. GAO (2023) finds families largely satisfied with quality but concerned about long waitlists, and notes little research on child outcomes (GAO-23-105518, not in the register). The National Women's Law Center documents the income-based fee schedule and pay tied to training.

statement: Gormley and others find Tulsa's universal pre-K raised kindergarten-entry scores by 0.79 standard deviations in letter-word identification, 0.64 in spelling and 0.38 in applied problems.
anchor: The authors found test impacts of 3.00 points (0.79 of the standard deviation for the control group) for the Letter-Word Identification score, 1.86 points (0.64 of the standard deviation of the control group) for the Spelling score, and 1.94 points (0.38 of the standard deviation of the control group) for the Applied Problems score.
context: Regression discontinuity (strong for the short run). Georgetown team.

statement: Gormley and others find college enrollment was 12 percentage points higher for Tulsa pre-K alumni than for students who attended neither Tulsa pre-K nor Head Start.
anchor: college enrollment was 12 percentage points higher for Tulsa pre-K alumni compared with former students who did not attend Tulsa pre-K or Head Start.
context: Observational (propensity weighting), weaker than a lottery; same Tulsa team as EV-CAR-555. Consistent with Boston's lottery result (EV-CAR-557).

statement: Gray-Lobe, Pathak and Walters find, from Boston's admissions lotteries, that public preschool raised college attendance, SAT-taking and high school graduation and cut disciplinary measures including juvenile incarceration, with no detectable effect on state test scores.
anchor: Preschool enrollment boosts college attendance as well as SAT test taking and high school graduation. Preschool also decreases high school disciplinary measures including juvenile incarceration, but has no detectable effect on state achievement test scores.
context: Lottery-based natural experiment (the strongest long-run U.S. design); Boston's program used a set curriculum and coaching, with cohorts from about 1997-2003. Independent of the Tulsa team. Contested on the short run by Tennessee (EV-CAR-559).

statement: The Tennessee Voluntary Pre-K randomized trial found pre-K children had lower state achievement scores in third through sixth grades than control children, strongest in sixth grade, and more disciplinary infractions, worse attendance and more special education.
anchor: had lower state achievement test scores in third through sixth grades than control children, with the strongest negative effects in sixth grade. A negative effect was also found for disciplinary infractions, attendance, and receipt of special education services, with null effects on retention.
context: Randomized trial (Vanderbilt team). Critics (NIEER, MDRC researchers) point to low measured classroom quality and low spending (about $4,524 a child in 2009); the authors answer that the program met standard structural benchmarks. The early gains faded by kindergarten (Lipsey and others, 2018).

statement: The Head Start Impact Study, a randomized trial, found access to Head Start improved children's preschool outcomes across developmental domains but had few impacts in kindergarten through third grade.
anchor: access to Head Start improved children's preschool outcomes across developmental domains, but had few impacts on children in kindergarten through 3rd grade.
context: HHS ACF, Obama administration, reporting a randomized trial run by independent contractors. Qualified by Kline and Walters (EV-CAR-561): about a third of the control group attended other preschools.

statement: Kline and Walters find Head Start draws about a third of its participants from other preschools, many publicly funded, and that counting this pushes Head Start's benefit-cost ratio well above one.
anchor: Head Start draws roughly a third of its participants from competing preschool programs, many of which receive public funds. We show that accounting for the fiscal impacts of such program substitution pushes estimates of Head Start's benefit-cost ratio well above one under a wide range of assumptions
context: Independent reanalysis of the federal trial.

statement: Deming finds Head Start participants gain 0.23 standard deviations on a summary index of young-adult outcomes, about 80 percent as large as model programs such as Perry Preschool, despite the fade-out of test score gains.
anchor: I estimate that Head Start participants gain 0.23 standard deviations on a summary index of young adult outcomes. This closes one-third of the gap between children with median and bottom quartile family income, and is about 80 percent as large as model programs such as Perry Preschool.
context: Sibling comparison (quasi-experimental); supported by Garces, Thomas and Currie (2002) and Bailey, Sun and Timpe (EV-CAR-563).

statement: Bailey, Sun and Timpe find Head Start's rollout raised adult schooling by 0.65 years, high school completion by 2.7 percent, college enrollment by 8.5 percent and college completion by 39 percent.
anchor: Head Start generated large increases in adult human capital and economic self-sufficiency, including a 0.65-year increase in schooling, a 2.7 percent increase in high school completion, an 8.5 percent increase in college enrollment, and a 39 percent increase in college completion.
context: Quasi-experimental (rollout timing); cohorts from the 1960s-70s, when the alternative was usually no preschool.

statement: García and others estimate the Abecedarian/CARE birth-to-five program's internal rate of return at 13.7%, with a benefit-cost ratio of 7.3.
anchor: Our point estimate of the internal rate of return is 13.7%, with an associated benefit/cost ratio of 7.3.
context: Small randomized trials plus forecasting; an intensive full-day program from infancy, unlike one year of pre-K. At scale, returns are smaller (WSIPP, EV-CAR-565).

statement: WSIPP estimates state pre-K for low-income children returns $4.78 in benefits per dollar of cost, with a 91% chance benefits exceed costs, mostly from earnings linked to test scores.
anchor: Benefit to cost ratio | $4.78 | Chance the program will produce | benefits greater than the costs | 91%
context: Nonpartisan state institute; excludes Perry and Abecedarian as small programs. Its benefits rest on test-score effects, the ones that fade (EV-CAR-560) or reverse (EV-CAR-559), so the ratio is uncertain.

statement: NIEER estimates high-quality full-day pre-K with pay parity costs about $12,500 per child a year on average, from $9,368 in Oklahoma to $16,221 in New York.
anchor: On average, the annual per child cost is about $12,500. But state-by-state rates ranged from $9,368 in Oklahoma to $16,221 in New York
context: Pre-K advocacy institute's cost model, 2020 dollars. Supported in scale by the National Academies' system cost (EV-CAR-567) and Maryland's $14,473 per pupil in FY2026 (not in the register).

statement: The National Academies estimate the total cost of high-quality early care and education for all children is at least $140 billion a year from all sources, about 0.75 percent of GDP, with public spending needing to rise by $5 billion to $53 billion a year over four phases.
anchor: the total cost of providing high quality ECE for all children is at least $140 billion per year (from all sources public and private), equivalent to about three-quarters of 1 percent (0.75 %) of U.S. gross domestic product
by at least $5 billion (in phase 1) to $53 billion (phase 4) a year above
context: Consensus cost model in 2016-18 dollars; parity with K-3 teachers adds about 10 percent. The $5-53 billion phases are in the same summary (quoted as "by at least $5 billion (in phase 1) to $53 billion (phase 4) a year above").

statement: Cascio and Schanzenbach find Georgia's and Oklahoma's universal pre-K raised lower-income children's test performance as late as eighth grade and the likelihood their mothers work, while among higher-income families it mostly shifted children from private to public preschool.
anchor: Among lower-income families, our findings also suggest that the programs have increased the amount of time mothers and children spend together on activities such as reading, the likelihood that mothers work, and children's test performance as late as eighth grade.
Among higher-income families, however, we find that the programs have shifted children from private to public pre-schools
context: Quasi-experimental. Cascio (2023, Journal of Human Resources) finds universal programs produce larger gains for low-income children than targeted ones.

statement: Brown estimates New York City's public pre-K reduced capacity for children under 2 at private child care centers by 2,700 seats, all in high-poverty areas, not offset by home-based care.
anchor: I estimate that the public pre-K program reduced the capacity for children younger than 2 years old at private child care centers by 2,700 seats. The entire decrease in capacity occurs in areas with high poverty, and this decline was not offset by an increase in provision in the home day care market.
context: A single working paper; another version of the paper gives 562 seats from the 2014 expansion and 2,248 extrapolated, so the size is uncertain. The mechanism (pre-K revenue cross-subsidizes infant rooms) is argued by the Bipartisan Policy Center and New America. The only quasi-experimental estimate found for the under-3 critique.

statement: The bipartisan Child Care Availability and Affordability Act (S. 847, March 4, 2025; Britt, Kaine and seven others) expands the employer-provided child care credit and the dependent care assistance exclusion; most of it passed in the 2025 law.

context: Bill text (a proposal).

statement: The CCDBG Act of 2014 established a 12-month eligibility period, so a child found eligible generally keeps assistance for a full year, and set a $1 million family asset limit.
anchor: established a 12-month eligibility period. This means that
once a child is deemed eligible, the child should generally
assets may not exceed $1 million.
2014 law added one new eligibility requirement: family
context: CRS (nonpartisan) on P.L. 113-186. The law also added background checks, health and safety training and annual inspections; it has not been reauthorized since.

statement: CLASP reports about 373,100 fewer children received CCDBG-funded child care in 2015 than in 2006, a 21 percent drop over nine years, as costs per child rose without matching funds.
anchor: Approximately 373,100 fewer children received CCDBG-funded child care in 2015 than in 2006, representing a 21 percent reduction in the average monthly number of children served over 9 years.
context: Advocacy group using HHS counts; the decline began before the 2014 law, so the law is one cause among several. An Oregon State University study found the new training and inspection rules were associated with a large drop in license-exempt nonrelative providers.

statement: CBO's official cost of the House Build Back Better Act's universal pre-K and child care for six years was $381 billion; CBO estimated $752 billion if made permanent.
anchor: Provide Universal Pre-K and Child Care for six years | $381 billion | $752 billion
context: CRFB tabulating CBO (official scorekeeper). CRFB's separate rows: child care $270 billion and pre-K $110 billion over six years. CBO assumed about a third of children live in states that would not take part (Bruenig, People's Policy Project), which lowers the cost. Penn Wharton put the pair at about $400 billion as written.

statement: Penn Wharton estimated the Build Back Better Act's child care and preschool provisions at $400 billion over ten years as proposed, plus $394 billion if made permanent.
anchor: Child care and pre-school | 400 | 394
context: Independent of CRFB and CBO; supports the scale.

statement: In December 2021 Senator Manchin said he would not vote for Build Back Better: "I cannot vote to continue with this piece of legislation."
anchor: I cannot vote to continue with this piece of legislation. I just can't. I tried everything humanly possible. I can't get there.
context: News report. His stated reasons were inflation, debt and temporary programs written to look cheaper, not the child care design itself.

statement: Niskanen's Stevens argues Build Back Better would have moved resources from nonparticipating to participating states, given large new benefits to relatively high-income families, and larger benefits to families in wealthier states.
anchor: BBB would have redistributed resources from nonparticipating to participating states, giving large new benefits to relatively high-income families, and providing larger benefits to families in wealthier states.
context: A critic's analysis. Supported in part by Bruenig (left) on the state-participation assumption in CBO's score.

statement: PERI cites an estimated cost of $60 billion a year for the 2025 Child Care for Working Families Act (universal preschool for 3- and 4-year-olds and a 7% copay cap for younger children).
anchor: The Child Care for Working Families Act introduced in 2025 proposed funding universal preschool for 3- to 4-year olds, and subsidizing child care costs for younger children at 7% of income for more working families, at an estimated cost of $60 billion per year.
context: An estimate cited without its method; CBO has not scored the bill. CAP put an earlier version at about $700 billion over ten years (2019). Qualified by CBO's Build Back Better scores (EV-CAR-587), a similar design.

statement: Child Trends finds the number of Vermont families receiving child care subsidies rose 55 percent, from 5,059 to 7,851, between July 2022 and May 2025, after the state widened eligibility and added a payroll tax to fund it.
anchor: The number of Vermont families receiving child care subsidies increased by 55 percent, rising from 5,059 to 7,851 from July 2022 to May 2025.
context: Program data reported by an independent research organization; not a causal evaluation. The payroll tax and eligibility levels are from Vermont's tax department and Act 76 (not in the register); care for children under 3 remains hard to find.

statement: Colorado appropriated $344 million for Universal Preschool in FY2024-25 ($197.7 million from its nicotine-tax preschool fund and $146.3 million general fund), for free hours in the year before kindergarten.
anchor: For FY 2024-25, the Legislature appropriated a total of $344 million for the Universal Preschool program, combining $197.7 million in Preschool Cash Funds with $146.3 million in General Funds.
context: State agency report; it funded 43,398 children. The 15-hour design is from the 2022 law (HB22-1295).

statement: CMS's 2024 rule required nursing homes to provide at least 3.48 total nurse staffing hours per resident day, including 0.55 registered-nurse hours and 2.45 nurse-aide hours.

statement: CMS estimated the 2024 standards would raise staffing in more than 79 percent of nursing facilities, cost $43.0 billion over 10 years ($4.30 billion a year on average), and require hiring about 16,000 registered nurses.

statement: In May 2024, 30 percent of 14,413 nursing homes staffed at or above the 2.45 nurse-aide minimum, 50 percent at or above the 0.55 registered-nurse minimum and 59 percent at or above the 3.48 total minimum; 78 percent provided at least 24 registered-nurse hours a day.

minimum (3.48 HPRD). Additionally, 78 percent of nursing homes provided at least 24 RN hours per day.

statement: KFF found that less than one in five (19%) nursing facilities met all three of the final rule's staffing minimums in late 2023.
anchor: Less than one in five (19%) of nursing facilities currently meet all three staffing minimums required in the final rule
context: KFF (independent nonprofit) analysis of Payroll-Based Journal data for October-December 2023.

statement: Abt Associates' study for CMS found that nursing home quality and safety rise with staffing levels with no obvious plateau or cliff, that registered-nurse staffing has the strongest relationship with quality, and that moving from a 3.30 to a 3.88 hours-per-resident-day minimum is associated with a 6-percentage-point rise in the share of homes predicted to exceed median quality.
anchor: quality and safety, as measured using claims, resident assessments, and health inspection data, increase with staffing levels, with no obvious plateau
RN staffing has the strongest relationship with nursing home quality and safety.
moving from the Low (3.30 total nurse staff HPRD) to Highest (3.88 nurse staff HPRD) nurse staff HPRD is associated with a 6-percentage point increase
context: CMS contractor study (Biden administration), observational and simulation analysis. Independent peer-reviewed work finds registered-nurse staffing matters most (EV-CAR-608) and that state minimums raised hours with mixed effects (EV-CAR-607).

statement: Chen and Grabowski find state minimum staffing standards raised total nursing hours per resident day by 5% on average and reduced severe deficiency citations, but lowered the direct-care skill mix because they treated all direct care staff alike.
anchor: minimum staffing standards increased total nursing hours per resident day by 5% on average. However, because the minimum staffing standards treated all direct care staff uniformly and ignored indirect care staff, the regulation had the unintended consequences of both lowering the direct care nursing skill mix
the staffing regulations led to a reduction in severe deficiency citations
context: Peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study (California and Ohio standards), academic authors.

statement: Lin, using eight states' 2000-2001 minimum staffing laws as natural experiments, finds registered-nurse staffing has a large and significant effect on nursing home quality and finds no significant association for nurse-aide staffing.
anchor: We exploit legislation changes regarding minimum staffing requirements in eight states between 2000 and 2001 as exogenous shocks to nurse staffing levels. We find that registered nurse staffing has a large and significant impact on quality of care, and that there is no evidence of a significant association between nurse aide staffing and quality of care.
context: Peer-reviewed instrumental-variables study, academic author.

statement: PHI counts nearly 5.4 million direct care workers in 2024, up from nearly 3.5 million in 2014, with a median hourly wage of $17.36 ($16.77 in home care); more than a third live in low-income households and 49 percent rely on public assistance.
anchor: growing from nearly 3.5 million workers in 2014 to nearly 5.4 million in 2024

context: PHI, a direct care workforce advocacy and research nonprofit, from ACS and BLS data. Its count is wider than BLS's aide category (EV-CAR-422) because it adds nursing assistants and residential aides. Thirty-six is written out in the source.

statement: Immigrants are 30% of the direct care workforce, against 18% of all adult workers; 33% in home care, 25% in nursing facilities and 23% in residential care facilities (2024).
anchor: Immigrants, including naturalized citizens and noncitizens, make up 30% of the overall direct care workforce, higher than the share of all adult workers in the U.S. who are immigrants (18%).

This analysis uses the 2024 American Community Survey

CMS has also delayed enforcement of a provision in the Medicaid Access Final Rule that would have required states to establish an advisory group
context: KFF, July 2026. The home care proposal is SRC-3130 (EV-CAR-616).

statement: Minnesota's Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board's minimum wages took effect September 10, 2026: $19.00 an hour for nursing home workers, $22.50 for certified nursing assistants, $23.50 for trained medication aides and $27.00 for licensed practical nurses, with a $1.50 increase on January 1, 2027; about 76% of certified nursing assistants get a raise.

about 76% of certified nursing assistants will get a raise
context: State agency announcement. The standards took effect after CMS approved Minnesota's Medicaid state plan amendment on August 11, 2026, which funds them through rates. A reported federal challenge by providers was not confirmed from a primary source.

context: State statute (RCW 74.39A.270), from Initiative 775 (2001). The state, as payer, bargains wages and the legislature funds them.

statement: The Supreme Court held in Harris v. Quinn that the First Amendment prohibits collecting an agency fee from Illinois Medicaid-funded personal assistants who do not want to join or support the union.
anchor: The First Amendment prohibits the collection of an agency fee from Rehabilitation Program PAs who do not want to join or support the union.
context: Holding; Janus v. AFSCME (2018) later extended the rule to all public employees (not in the register). Bargaining itself remains lawful.

statement: Ruffini finds that a ten percent increase in the minimum wage raises low-skilled nursing home workers' earnings one to two percent, reduces separations and would prevent at least 15,000 deaths, lowering inspection violations by one to two percent, with no significant change in profitability.
anchor: I find that a ten percent increase in the minimum wage raises low-skilled nursing home workers’ earnings one to two percent, reduces separations, and increases stable hires.
A ten percent increase in the minimum wage would prevent at least 15,000 deaths, lower the number of inspection violations by one to two percent
resulting in no significant change in profitability
context: Quasi-experimental (state minimum wage reforms). Working paper read; the peer-reviewed version (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2024) may differ. Funder: Washington Center for Equitable Growth (progressive). Howes's home care study points the same way (EV-CAR-625).

statement: Howes finds the annual retention rate of new San Francisco home care providers rose from 39 percent to 74 percent after significant wage and benefit increases, and estimates a $1 raise from $8 an hour would increase retention by 17 percentage points.
anchor: the annual retention rate of new providers rose from 39 percent to 74 percent following significant wage and benefit increases and that a $1 increase in the wage rate from $8 an hour—the national average wage for homecare—would increase retention by 17 percentage points
context: Peer-reviewed; before-and-after and regression evidence from one county's IHSS program after bargaining raised wages, not a randomized or difference-in-differences design. Urban's DC evaluation (EV-CAR-550) and Ruffini (EV-CAR-624) point the same way.

statement: LeadingAge's LTSS Center estimates that raising all direct care workers to a living wage in 2022 would give 75.3% of them a raise averaging 15.5% at a cost of about $9.4 billion, with turnover lower by only 0.7 to 1.7 percentage points; its summary says lower turnover and higher productivity would offset most, if not all, of the cost.
anchor: Raising pay to a living wage in 2022 will give 75.3% of direct care workers a higher wage than they would otherwise receive.
the average wage gain for workers receiving a pay increase would be 15.5%
estimated to be $9.4 billion
Higher pay would result in a modest reduction in turnover of between 0.7 and 1.7 percentage points.
Lower turnover and higher productivity would offset most, if not all, of the costs of higher pay.
context: Provider trade association with UMass Boston (a stake in higher Medicaid rates). Its own numbers do not support the headline offset: turnover savings are put at "possibly covering more than 10% of the total wage increase" in the same summary, and the offset rests mainly on a productivity estimate. The project uses its cost, not its offset. The $9.4 billion is the raise for workers below a living wage, not a floor above it.

statement: In the randomized HPOG evaluation, access to the program raised employment in a healthcare occupation six years later from 32 percent to 37 percent and receipt of any postsecondary credential from 70 to 78 percent, but did not detectably raise quarterly earnings.
anchor: HPOG increased employment in a healthcare occupation by 5 percentage points, from 32 percent in the control group to 37 percent in the group that could access the program.

context: Randomized trial run for HHS (OPRE Report 2022-45) by its evaluator, Abt Associates. Most HPOG training was short-term, and the control group could get similar courses. Sector-training trials with job placement show larger earnings gains (EV-CAR-632).

statement: A review of randomized evaluations of sector-focused training programs for low-wage workers finds substantial and persistent earnings gains of 11 to 40 percent after training.
anchor: The programs generate substantial and persistent earnings gains (11 to 40 percent) following training completion.
context: NBER working paper (Katz, Roth, Hendra and Schaberg); two authors at MDRC, which ran one of the trials. The programs mostly trained for IT, manufacturing and health jobs with higher pay than direct care; HPOG's health-care result is weaker (EV-CAR-631).
